questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
Which of the following subspaces must be orthogonal to $\text{Col}(A)$ for every matrix $A?$

I. $\text{Col}({A}^{T})$

II. $\text{Null}({A}^{T})$

III. $\text{Null}(A)$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that $\text{Col}(A)$ consists of all linear combinations of the columns of $A$, that is, the rows of ${A}^{T}.$

If a vector is orthogonal to every linear combination of the rows of ${A}^{T},$ it must be orthogonal to each row of ${A}^{T}.$
But notice that when pre-multiplying a vector by ${A}^{T},$ we actually multiply each row of ${A}^{T}$ by that vector.
So, $\text{Col}(A)$ must be orthogonal to the left null space of $A,$ which is $\text{Null}({A}^{T}).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

**Note:** In general, the four fundamental subspaces of a matrix $A$ can be schematically visualized, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14154359/assets/de22dd5b352e1d5be48f4b6ed3b2a4657ae623c1bd288d3464559758ea334af7.png)

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
Which of the following subspaces must be orthogonal to $\text{Null}({A}^{T})$ for every matrix $A?$

I. $\text{Col}(A)$

II. $\text{Null}(A)$

III. $\text{Col}({A}^{T})$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that $\text{Null}({A}^{T})$ is the left null space of $A.$ This consists of vectors that, when pre-multiplied by ${A}^{T},$ result in the zero-vector $0.$

When pre-multiplying a vector by ${A}^{T},$ we actually multiply each row of ${A}^{T}$, that is, each column of $A$, by that vector. So, $\text{Null}({A}^{T})$ must be orthogonal to the column space of $A,$ which is $\text{Col}(A).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

**Note:** In general, the four fundamental subspaces of a matrix $A$ can be schematically visualized, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14154359/assets/de22dd5b352e1d5be48f4b6ed3b2a4657ae623c1bd288d3464559758ea334af7.png)

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
Which of the following subspaces must be orthogonal to $\text{Null}(A+B)$ for all compatible matrices $A$ and $B?$

I. $\text{Null}({A}^{T}+{B}^{T})$

II. $\text{Col}({A}^{T}+{B}^{T})$

III. $\text{Col}(A+B)$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that $\text{Null}(A+B)$ contains all vectors that, when pre-multiplied by $A+B,$ result in the zero-vector $0.$ 

When pre-multiplying a vector by $A+B,$ we actually multiply each row of $A+B$ by that vector. So, $\text{Null}(A+B)$ must be orthogonal to the row space of $A+B,$ which is $\text{Col}((A+B)^{T})=\text{Col}({A}^{T}+{B}^{T}).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

So, $\text{Col}({B}^{T})$ must be orthogonal to the null space of $B,$ which is $\text{Null}(B).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

questions.name: Question 6
questions.problem: Let $A$ and $B$ be $m\times p$ and $p\times n$ matrices, respectively. What is the image of $\text{Col}({B}^{T}\,{A}^{T})$ under the action of $AB?$
questions.worked_solution:
Pre-multiplying a vector $x\in {R}^{n}$ by $AB$ gives a linear combination of the columns of $AB:$

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}| & | & ⋯ & | \\ (ab)_{1} & (ab)_{2} & ⋯ & (ab)_{n} \\ | & | & ⋯ & |\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{AB}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}={x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}| \\ (ab)_{1} \\ |\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}| \\ (ab)_{2} \\ |\end{aligned}]+⋯+{x}_{n}[\begin{aligned}| \\ (ab)_{n} \\ |\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore, the image of ${R}^{n}$ under the action of $AB$ must be $\text{Col}(AB),$ the column space of $AB.$

Furthermore, since $\text{Null}(AB)$ is mapped to the zero vector $0$ by the definition of the null subspace, the image of its orthogonal complement $\text{Col}((AB)^{T})=\text{Col}({B}^{T}\,{A}^{T})$ must be $\text{Col}(AB).$

This can be schematically visualized, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14154359/assets/885bf8a3061f93ad400897a7273ffe4157d22dee20b8e4ee7ebb982b1c4319bb.png)

questions.name: Question 8
questions.problem: Let $A$ be a $7\times 5$ matrix. What is the image of ${R}^{5}$ under the action of $A?$
questions.worked_solution:
Pre-multiplying a vector $x\in {R}^{5}$ by $A$ gives a linear combination of the columns of $A:$

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} & {a}_{3} & {a}_{4} & {a}_{5} \\ | & | & | & | & |\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{4} \\ {x}_{5}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}={x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}| \\ {a}_{1} \\ |\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}| \\ {a}_{2} \\ |\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}| \\ {a}_{3} \\ |\end{aligned}]+{x}_{4}[\begin{aligned}| \\ {a}_{4} \\ |\end{aligned}]+{x}_{5}[\begin{aligned}| \\ {a}_{5} \\ |\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore, the image of ${R}^{5}$ under the action of $A$ must be $\text{Col}(A),$ the column space of $A.$

questions.name: Question 10
questions.problem: Let $A$ and $B$ be $m\times n$ matrices. What is the image of ${R}^{m}$ under the action of ${A}^{T}+{B}^{T}?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that ${A}^{T}+{B}^{T}$ is a $n\times m$ matrix.

Now, pre-multiplying a vector $x\in {R}^{m}$ by ${A}^{T}+{B}^{T}$ gives a linear combination of the columns of ${A}^{T}+{B}^{T}:$

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}| & | & ⋯ & | \\ ({a}^{T}+{b}^{T})_{1} & ({a}^{T}+{b}^{T})_{2} & ⋯ & ({a}^{T}+{b}^{T})_{m} \\ | & | & ⋯ & |\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{T}+{B}^{T}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{m}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}={x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}| \\ ({a}^{T}+{b}^{T})_{1} \\ |\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}| \\ ({a}^{T}+{b}^{T})_{2} \\ |\end{aligned}]+⋯+{x}_{m}[\begin{aligned}| \\ ({a}^{T}+{b}^{T})_{m} \\ |\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore, the image of ${R}^{m}$ under the action of ${A}^{T}+{B}^{T}$ must be $\text{Col}({A}^{T}+{B}^{T}),$ the row space of $A+B.$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Identifying an Orthogonal Fundamental Subspaces of a Matrix
canonical_examples.problem:
Which of the following subspaces must be orthogonal to $\text{Col}(A^T)$ for every matrix $A?$

I. $\text{Null}(A)$

II. $\text{Col}(A)$

III. $\text{Null}(A^T)$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that $\text{Col}(A^T)$ is the row space of $A,$ and consists of all linear combinations of the rows of $A.$

If a vector is orthogonal to every linear combination of the rows of $A,$ it must be orthogonal to each row of $A.$
But notice that when pre-multiplying a vector by $A,$ we multiply each row of $A$ by that vector.
So, $\text{Col}(A^T)$ must be orthogonal to the null space of $A,$ which is $\text{Null}(A).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

**Note:** In general, the four fundamental subspaces of a matrix $A$ can be schematically visualized, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14154359/assets/de22dd5b352e1d5be48f4b6ed3b2a4657ae623c1bd288d3464559758ea334af7.png)
canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Identifying an Orthogonal Fundamental Subspaces of a Matrix

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Identifying the Images of the Four Fundamental Subspaces of the Matrix Under Its Action
canonical_examples.problem: Let $A$ be a $m \times n$ matrix. What is the image of $\text{Col}(A^T)$ under the action of $A?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Pre-multiplying a vector $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ by $A$ gives a linear combination of the columns of $A{:}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14154359/assets/dc853850b03dd2cf8fcf0168392e3490423725120b6acb55f88028a702d30fa5.svg)

Therefore, the image of $\mathbb{R}^n$ under the action of $A$ must be $\text{Col}(A),$ the column space of $A.$

Furthermore, since $\text{Null}(A)$ is mapped to the zero vector $\mathbf{0}$ by the definition of the null subspace, the image of its orthogonal complement $\text{Col}(A^T)$ must be $\text{Col}(A).$

This can be schematically visualized, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14154359/assets/8b08bdf79d53f312cabd665bcd4669795bd8851dfb33d5e5db6178bd80b24398.png)

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding the Dimensions of the Four Fundamental Subspaces of a Matrix
canonical_examples.problem: Consider a $8 \times 6$ matrix $A.$ If $\text{dim}(\text{Null}(A)) = 3,$ then find $\text{dim}(\text{Col}(A^T)).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The four fundamental subspaces of a matrix $A$ can be schematically visualized, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14154359/assets/889b83fadd26b377c4dd34143c9b16541630c04e90de3d9b005e7147ead75ad5.png)

In our case, we are given that $m=8,$ $n=6,$ and $n-r=3.$ 

Substituting $n=6$ into $n-r=3,$ we can find the rank of $A{:}$

$$
6 - r = 3 
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
r = 3
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{dim}(\text{Col}({A}^{T})) & =r=3.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
When considering an $m \times n$ matrix $A$ as a linear transformation

$$
\mathbb{R}^n \xrightarrow{\quad A \quad} \mathbb{R}^m,
$$

there are **four fundamental subspaces** that naturally occur. The first two are as follows:

- The **column space** of $A,$ denoted $\text{Col}(A),$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^m.$ This is the set of all linear combinations of the columns of $A.$

- The **null space** of $A,$ denoted $\text{Null}(A),$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^n.$ This is the set of all vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$ that, when pre-multiplied by $A,$ result in the zero-vector $\mathbf{0}.$

Now, notice that the transpose $A^T$ is an $n \times m$ matrix and can be considered as the transformation 

$$
\mathbb{R}^m \xrightarrow{\quad A^T \quad} \mathbb{R}^n.
$$

So, we have similar subspaces for the transpose $A^T{:}$

- The column space of $A^T,$ denoted $\text{Col}(A^T),$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^n.$ We call this the **row space** of $A$ since the span of the columns of $A^T$ is equivalent to the span of the rows of $A.$

- The null space of $A^T,$ denoted $\text{Null}(A^T),$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^m.$ We call this the **left null space** of $A$ since it is equivalent to the set of all vectors $\mathbf y\in\mathbb R^m$ such that $\mathbf y^T A = \mathbf{0}.$

Let's discuss how these spaces relate to each other:

- We have two subspaces in $\mathbb{R}^n$ that are orthogonal complements of each other:

$$
\text{Col}(A^T) = \text{Null}(A)^\perp
$$

- We have two subspaces in $\mathbb{R}^m$ that are orthogonal complements of each other:

$$
\text{Col}(A) = \text{Null}(A^T)^\perp
$$

The four fundamental subspaces of a matrix $A$ can be schematically visualized, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14154359/assets/ced4191955b6886491bf612c62344d2faf6e7fe8d49884446de0eb86851d22e8.png)

To see why $\text{Col}(A)$ is the orthogonal complement of $\text{Null}(A^T),$ note the following:

- When calculating the product $A^T \mathbf x,$ we multiply each row of $A^T$ by $\mathbf x.$

- Suppose that $\mathbf x\in \text{Null}(A^T).$ Then, by definition, $A^T \mathbf x = \mathbf 0.$

- Thus, $\mathbf x$ must be orthogonal to each row of $A^T.$ Equivalently, this means that $\mathbf x$ is orthogonal to each *column* of $A.$

- Hence, $\text{Null}(A^T)$ is orthogonal to $\text{Col}(A).$

We can deduce that $\text{Null}(A)$ is the orthogonal complement of $\text{Col}(A^T)$ by similar reasoning.

tutorials.name: Images Under the Action of a Matrix and Its Transpose
tutorials.problem:
Given an $m \times n$ matrix $A,$ what is the image of $\mathbb{R}^n$ under $A?$

Note that pre-multiplying a vector $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ by $A$ gives a linear combination of the columns of $A{:}$
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14154359/assets/a3cf2fb6734efe387ad41c59743385154d7a172d2cc10ee0fe69ac6a7f2b342a.svg)

Therefore, by definition, the image of $\mathbb{R}^n$ under the action of $A$ is $\text{Col}(A),$ the column space of $A.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14154359/assets/dbefb436195af5ffa8841f4119054426db50ac2987138a5912991cf42321e0dc.png)

Similarly, pre-multiplying a vector $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^m$ by $A^T$ gives a linear combination of the columns of $A^T{:}$
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14154359/assets/60574ae7f9fc09522e9d725c787dce63228c67e19cbef002b14e29c1f27e4b20.svg)

Therefore, the image of $\mathbb{R}^m$ under the action of $A^T$ must be $\text{Col}(A^T).$ This is also the row space of $A,$ since a linear combination of the columns of $A^T$ is equivalent to a linear combination of the rows of $A.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14154359/assets/c82ab88289fc2d35ce354933937d908c54a9839bfa0fd126187a9723c58eeb27.png)

We can use similar reasoning to find the image of the four fundamental subspaces under the appropriate matrix.

tutorials.content:
Given an $m \times n$ matrix $A,$ what is the image of $\mathbb{R}^n$ under $A?$

Note that pre-multiplying a vector $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ by $A$ gives a linear combination of the columns of $A{:}$
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14154359/assets/a3cf2fb6734efe387ad41c59743385154d7a172d2cc10ee0fe69ac6a7f2b342a.svg)

Therefore, by definition, the image of $\mathbb{R}^n$ under the action of $A$ is $\text{Col}(A),$ the column space of $A.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14154359/assets/dbefb436195af5ffa8841f4119054426db50ac2987138a5912991cf42321e0dc.png)

Similarly, pre-multiplying a vector $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^m$ by $A^T$ gives a linear combination of the columns of $A^T{:}$
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14154359/assets/60574ae7f9fc09522e9d725c787dce63228c67e19cbef002b14e29c1f27e4b20.svg)

Therefore, the image of $\mathbb{R}^m$ under the action of $A^T$ must be $\text{Col}(A^T).$ This is also the row space of $A,$ since a linear combination of the columns of $A^T$ is equivalent to a linear combination of the rows of $A.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14154359/assets/c82ab88289fc2d35ce354933937d908c54a9839bfa0fd126187a9723c58eeb27.png)

We can use similar reasoning to find the image of the four fundamental subspaces under the appropriate matrix.

tutorials.name: Dimensions of the Four Fundamental Subspaces
tutorials.problem:
Consider an $m \times n$ matrix $A$ with rank $r.$ The dimensions of the four fundamental subspaces of $A$ are as follows:

- $\text{dim}(\text{Col}(A)) = r.$ Since the column space is the span of the columns of $A,$ its dimension is the number of linearly independent columns which, by Gaussian elimination, is $\text{rank}(A)=r.$

- $\text{dim}(\text{Col}(A^T)) = r.$ It can be shown that the dimension of the row space of $A$ also equals $r.$ Therefore, $\text{rank}(A^T)=\text{rank}(A)=r.$

- $\text{dim}(\text{Null}(A)) = n-r.$ Since $\text{Null}(A)$ is the orthogonal complement of $\text{Col}(A^T)$ in $\mathbb{R}^n,$ we have that

$$
\text{dim}(\text{Null}(A)) = \underbrace{\text{dim}(\mathbb{R}^n)}_{n} - \underbrace{\text{dim}(\text{Col}(A^T))}_{r} = n-r.
$$

- $\text{dim}(\text{Null}(A^T)) = m-r.$ Since $\text{Null}(A^T)$ is the orthogonal complement of $\text{Col}(A)$ in $\mathbb{R}^m,$ we have that

$$
\text{dim}(\text{Null}(A^T)) = \underbrace{\text{dim}(\mathbb{R}^m)}_{m} - \underbrace{\text{dim}(\text{Col}(A))}_{r} = m-r.
$$

Let's add these dimensions to the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14154359/assets/1c550b87048bba6a7c362f00f09faca74ca9b056a93698436d0994c120971356.png)

tutorials.name: The Big Picture of the Four Fundamental Subspaces
tutorials.problem:
Let's review what we have learned in this lesson.

If we consider an $m \times n$ matrix $A$ of rank $r$ as a transformation from $\mathbb{R}^n$ to $\mathbb{R}^m,$ then there are four fundamental subspaces of $A{:}$

- $\text{Col}(A)$ and $\text{Null}(A^T)$ are subspaces in $\mathbb{R}^m$ with dimensions $r$ and $m-r,$ respectively.

- $\text{Col}(A^T)$ and $\text{Null}(A)$ are subspaces in $\mathbb{R}^n$ with dimensions $r$ and $n-r,$ respectively.

Furthermore,

- $\text{Col}(A)$ and $\text{Null}(A^T)$ are orthogonal complements in $\mathbb{R}^m,$ and

- $\text{Null}(A)$ and $\text{Col}(A^T)$ are orthogonal complements in $\mathbb{R}^n.$

Finally, we have that

- the image of $\text{Col}(A^T)$ under the action of $A$ is $\text{Col}(A),$ and

- the image of $\text{Col}(A)$ under the action of $A^T$ is $\text{Col}(A^T).$

These facts about the four fundamental subspaces of a matrix $A$ can be schematically visualized, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14154359/assets/37f633d0bca1a599f7d1658c051f802da5d607d420beeb4bddbef5cd98c366ef.png)

tutorial.name: Introduction
tutorial.problem:
When considering an $m \times n$ matrix $A$ as a linear transformation

$$
\mathbb{R}^n \xrightarrow{\quad A \quad} \mathbb{R}^m,
$$

there are **four fundamental subspaces** that naturally occur. The first two are as follows:

- The **column space** of $A,$ denoted $\text{Col}(A),$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^m.$ This is the set of all linear combinations of the columns of $A.$

- The **null space** of $A,$ denoted $\text{Null}(A),$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^n.$ This is the set of all vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$ that, when pre-multiplied by $A,$ result in the zero-vector $\mathbf{0}.$

Now, notice that the transpose $A^T$ is an $n \times m$ matrix and can be considered as the transformation 

$$
\mathbb{R}^m \xrightarrow{\quad A^T \quad} \mathbb{R}^n.
$$

So, we have similar subspaces for the transpose $A^T{:}$

- The column space of $A^T,$ denoted $\text{Col}(A^T),$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^n.$ We call this the **row space** of $A$ since the span of the columns of $A^T$ is equivalent to the span of the rows of $A.$

- The null space of $A^T,$ denoted $\text{Null}(A^T),$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^m.$ We call this the **left null space** of $A$ since it is equivalent to the set of all vectors $\mathbf y\in\mathbb R^m$ such that $\mathbf y^T A = \mathbf{0}.$

Let's discuss how these spaces relate to each other:

- We have two subspaces in $\mathbb{R}^n$ that are orthogonal complements of each other:

$$
\text{Col}(A^T) = \text{Null}(A)^\perp
$$

- We have two subspaces in $\mathbb{R}^m$ that are orthogonal complements of each other:

$$
\text{Col}(A) = \text{Null}(A^T)^\perp
$$

The four fundamental subspaces of a matrix $A$ can be schematically visualized, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14154359/assets/ced4191955b6886491bf612c62344d2faf6e7fe8d49884446de0eb86851d22e8.png)

To see why $\text{Col}(A)$ is the orthogonal complement of $\text{Null}(A^T),$ note the following:

- When calculating the product $A^T \mathbf x,$ we multiply each row of $A^T$ by $\mathbf x.$

- Suppose that $\mathbf x\in \text{Null}(A^T).$ Then, by definition, $A^T \mathbf x = \mathbf 0.$

- Thus, $\mathbf x$ must be orthogonal to each row of $A^T.$ Equivalently, this means that $\mathbf x$ is orthogonal to each *column* of $A.$

- Hence, $\text{Null}(A^T)$ is orthogonal to $\text{Col}(A).$

We can deduce that $\text{Null}(A)$ is the orthogonal complement of $\text{Col}(A^T)$ by similar reasoning.

question.problem:
Which of the following subspaces must be orthogonal to $\text{Col}(A^T)$ for every matrix $A?$

I. $\text{Null}(A)$

II. $\text{Col}(A)$

III. $\text{Null}(A^T)$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that $\text{Col}(A^T)$ is the row space of $A,$ and consists of all linear combinations of the rows of $A.$

If a vector is orthogonal to every linear combination of the rows of $A,$ it must be orthogonal to each row of $A.$
But notice that when pre-multiplying a vector by $A,$ we multiply each row of $A$ by that vector.
So, $\text{Col}(A^T)$ must be orthogonal to the null space of $A,$ which is $\text{Null}(A).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

**Note:** In general, the four fundamental subspaces of a matrix $A$ can be schematically visualized, as shown below.

tutorial.name: Images Under the Action of a Matrix and Its Transpose
tutorial.problem:
Given an $m \times n$ matrix $A,$ what is the image of $\mathbb{R}^n$ under $A?$

Note that pre-multiplying a vector $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ by $A$ gives a linear combination of the columns of $A{:}$
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14154359/assets/83cbcf9ae413191a590ea1ef26528bab4364058b92f066f259f18b7886fc8083.svg)

Therefore, by definition, the image of $\mathbb{R}^n$ under the action of $A$ is $\text{Col}(A),$ the column space of $A.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14154359/assets/dbefb436195af5ffa8841f4119054426db50ac2987138a5912991cf42321e0dc.png)

Similarly, pre-multiplying a vector $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^m$ by $A^T$ gives a linear combination of the columns of $A^T{:}$
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14154359/assets/e70a345f29cd60b00d50edd684320fc73c7f93eff1ca8f320b11ace44fe05055.svg)

Therefore, the image of $\mathbb{R}^m$ under the action of $A^T$ must be $\text{Col}(A^T).$ This is also the row space of $A,$ since a linear combination of the columns of $A^T$ is equivalent to a linear combination of the rows of $A.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14154359/assets/c82ab88289fc2d35ce354933937d908c54a9839bfa0fd126187a9723c58eeb27.png)

We can use similar reasoning to find the image of the four fundamental subspaces under the appropriate matrix.

tutorial.content:
Given an $m \times n$ matrix $A,$ what is the image of $\mathbb{R}^n$ under $A?$

Note that pre-multiplying a vector $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ by $A$ gives a linear combination of the columns of $A{:}$
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14154359/assets/83cbcf9ae413191a590ea1ef26528bab4364058b92f066f259f18b7886fc8083.svg)

Therefore, by definition, the image of $\mathbb{R}^n$ under the action of $A$ is $\text{Col}(A),$ the column space of $A.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14154359/assets/dbefb436195af5ffa8841f4119054426db50ac2987138a5912991cf42321e0dc.png)

Similarly, pre-multiplying a vector $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^m$ by $A^T$ gives a linear combination of the columns of $A^T{:}$
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14154359/assets/e70a345f29cd60b00d50edd684320fc73c7f93eff1ca8f320b11ace44fe05055.svg)

Therefore, the image of $\mathbb{R}^m$ under the action of $A^T$ must be $\text{Col}(A^T).$ This is also the row space of $A,$ since a linear combination of the columns of $A^T$ is equivalent to a linear combination of the rows of $A.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14154359/assets/c82ab88289fc2d35ce354933937d908c54a9839bfa0fd126187a9723c58eeb27.png)

We can use similar reasoning to find the image of the four fundamental subspaces under the appropriate matrix.

tutorial.name: Dimensions of the Four Fundamental Subspaces
tutorial.problem:
Consider an $m \times n$ matrix $A$ with rank $r.$ The dimensions of the four fundamental subspaces of $A$ are as follows:

- $\text{dim}(\text{Col}(A)) = r.$ Since the column space is the span of the columns of $A,$ its dimension is the number of linearly independent columns which, by Gaussian elimination, is $\text{rank}(A)=r.$

- $\text{dim}(\text{Col}(A^T)) = r.$ It can be shown that the dimension of the row space of $A$ also equals $r.$ Therefore, $\text{rank}(A^T)=\text{rank}(A)=r.$

- $\text{dim}(\text{Null}(A)) = n-r.$ Since $\text{Null}(A)$ is the orthogonal complement of $\text{Col}(A^T)$ in $\mathbb{R}^n,$ we have that

$$
\text{dim}(\text{Null}(A)) = \underbrace{\text{dim}(\mathbb{R}^n)}_{n} - \underbrace{\text{dim}(\text{Col}(A^T))}_{r} = n-r.
$$

- $\text{dim}(\text{Null}(A^T)) = m-r.$ Since $\text{Null}(A^T)$ is the orthogonal complement of $\text{Col}(A)$ in $\mathbb{R}^m,$ we have that

$$
\text{dim}(\text{Null}(A^T)) = \underbrace{\text{dim}(\mathbb{R}^m)}_{m} - \underbrace{\text{dim}(\text{Col}(A))}_{r} = m-r.
$$

Let's add these dimensions to the diagram below.

tutorial.name: The Big Picture of the Four Fundamental Subspaces
tutorial.problem:
Let's review what we have learned in this lesson.

If we consider an $m \times n$ matrix $A$ of rank $r$ as a transformation from $\mathbb{R}^n$ to $\mathbb{R}^m,$ then there are four fundamental subspaces of $A{:}$

- $\text{Col}(A)$ and $\text{Null}(A^T)$ are subspaces in $\mathbb{R}^m$ with dimensions $r$ and $m-r,$ respectively.

- $\text{Col}(A^T)$ and $\text{Null}(A)$ are subspaces in $\mathbb{R}^n$ with dimensions $r$ and $n-r,$ respectively.

Furthermore,

- $\text{Col}(A)$ and $\text{Null}(A^T)$ are orthogonal complements in $\mathbb{R}^m,$ and

- $\text{Null}(A)$ and $\text{Col}(A^T)$ are orthogonal complements in $\mathbb{R}^n.$

Finally, we have that

- the image of $\text{Col}(A^T)$ under the action of $A$ is $\text{Col}(A),$ and

- the image of $\text{Col}(A)$ under the action of $A^T$ is $\text{Col}(A^T).$

These facts about the four fundamental subspaces of a matrix $A$ can be schematically visualized, as shown below.

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
Which of the following subspaces must be orthogonal to $\text{Col}(A)$ for every matrix $A?$

I. $\text{Col}({A}^{T})$

II. $\text{Null}({A}^{T})$

III. $\text{Null}(A)$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that $\text{Col}(A)$ consists of all linear combinations of the columns of $A$, that is, the rows of ${A}^{T}.$

If a vector is orthogonal to every linear combination of the rows of ${A}^{T},$ it must be orthogonal to each row of ${A}^{T}.$
But notice that when pre-multiplying a vector by ${A}^{T},$ we actually multiply each row of ${A}^{T}$ by that vector.
So, $\text{Col}(A)$ must be orthogonal to the left null space of $A,$ which is $\text{Null}({A}^{T}).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

**Note:** In general, the four fundamental subspaces of a matrix $A$ can be schematically visualized, as shown below.

question.name: Question 6
question.problem: Let $A$ and $B$ be $m\times p$ and $p\times n$ matrices, respectively. What is the image of $\text{Col}({B}^{T}\,{A}^{T})$ under the action of $AB?$
question.worked_solution:
Pre-multiplying a vector $x\in {R}^{n}$ by $AB$ gives a linear combination of the columns of $AB:$

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}| & | & ⋯ & | \\ (ab)_{1} & (ab)_{2} & ⋯ & (ab)_{n} \\ | & | & ⋯ & |\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{AB}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}={x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}| \\ (ab)_{1} \\ |\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}| \\ (ab)_{2} \\ |\end{aligned}]+⋯+{x}_{n}[\begin{aligned}| \\ (ab)_{n} \\ |\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore, the image of ${R}^{n}$ under the action of $AB$ must be $\text{Col}(AB),$ the column space of $AB.$

Furthermore, since $\text{Null}(AB)$ is mapped to the zero vector $0$ by the definition of the null subspace, the image of its orthogonal complement $\text{Col}((AB)^{T})=\text{Col}({B}^{T}\,{A}^{T})$ must be $\text{Col}(AB).$

question.html:
Question 6
?

Let A and B be m×p and p×n matrices, respectively. What is the image of Col(BTAT) under the action of AB?

a
Null(AB)
b
Col(AB)
c
Null(BTAT)
d
Col(BTAT)
e
0
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Pre-multiplying a vector x∈Rn by AB gives a linear combination of the columns of AB:

[||⋯|(ab)1(ab)2⋯(ab)n||⋯|]⏟AB⋅[x1⋮xn]⏟x=x1[|(ab)1|]+x2[|(ab)2|]+⋯+xn[|(ab)n|]

Therefore, the image of Rn under the action of AB must be Col(AB), the column space of AB.

Furthermore, since Null(AB) is mapped to the zero vector 0 by the definition of the null subspace, the image of its orthogonal complement Col((AB)T)=Col(BTAT) must be Col(AB).

This can be schematically visualized, as shown below.

last_observation.worked_solution:
Pre-multiplying a vector $x\in {R}^{n}$ by $A+B$ gives a linear combination of the columns of $A+B:$

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}| & | & ⋯ & | \\ (a+b)_{1} & (a+b)_{2} & ⋯ & (a+b)_{n} \\ | & | & ⋯ & |\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A+B}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}={x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}| \\ (a+b)_{1} \\ |\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}| \\ (a+b)_{2} \\ |\end{aligned}]+⋯+{x}_{n}[\begin{aligned}| \\ (a+b)_{n} \\ |\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore, the image of ${R}^{n}$ under the action of $A+B$ must be $\text{Col}(A+B),$ the column space of $A+B.$

Furthermore, since $\text{Null}(A+B)$ is mapped to the zero vector $0$ by the definition of the null subspace, the image of its orthogonal complement $\text{Col}((A+B)^{T})=\text{Col}({A}^{T}+{B}^{T})$ must be $\text{Col}(A+B).$

Question 7
?

Let A and B be m×n matrices. What is the image of Col(AT+BT) under the action of A+B?

a
Null(AT+BT)
b
0
c
Col(A+B)
d
Null(A+B)
e
Col(AT+BT)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Pre-multiplying a vector x∈Rn by A+B gives a linear combination of the columns of A+B:

[||⋯|(a+b)1(a+b)2⋯(a+b)n||⋯|]⏟A+B⋅[x1⋮xn]⏟x=x1[|(a+b)1|]+x2[|(a+b)2|]+⋯+xn[|(a+b)n|]

Therefore, the image of Rn under the action of A+B must be Col(A+B), the column space of A+B.

Furthermore, since Null(A+B) is mapped to the zero vector 0 by the definition of the null subspace, the image of its orthogonal complement Col((A+B)T)=Col(AT+BT) must be Col(A+B).

This can be schematically visualized, as shown below.

solution.reasoning: Let M=A+B, so M^T=A^T+B^T. Every x in R^n decomposes as x=r+k with r in Col(M^T) and k in Null(M). Since Mx=Mr, the image of Col(M^T) under M equals the full image Col(M). Therefore the answer is Col(A+B), option c. The supplied example supports this theorem but does not capture Math Academy's answer to the current question.

Question 8

Let A be a 7×5 matrix. What is the image of R5 under the action of A?

a
R7
b
Col(A)
c
R5
d
0
e
Null(A)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Pre-multiplying a vector x∈R5 by A gives a linear combination of the columns of A:

[|||||a1a2a3a4a5|||||]⏟A⋅[x1x2x3x4x5]⏟x=x1[|a1|]+x2[|a2|]+x3[|a3|]+x4[|a4|]+x5[|a5|]

Therefore, the image of R5 under the action of A must be Col(A), the column space of A.

question.name: Question 10
question.problem: Let $A$ and $B$ be $m\times n$ matrices. What is the image of ${R}^{m}$ under the action of ${A}^{T}+{B}^{T}?$
question.worked_solution:
First, notice that ${A}^{T}+{B}^{T}$ is a $n\times m$ matrix.

Now, pre-multiplying a vector $x\in {R}^{m}$ by ${A}^{T}+{B}^{T}$ gives a linear combination of the columns of ${A}^{T}+{B}^{T}:$

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}| & | & ⋯ & | \\ ({a}^{T}+{b}^{T})_{1} & ({a}^{T}+{b}^{T})_{2} & ⋯ & ({a}^{T}+{b}^{T})_{m} \\ | & | & ⋯ & |\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{T}+{B}^{T}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{m}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}={x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}| \\ ({a}^{T}+{b}^{T})_{1} \\ |\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}| \\ ({a}^{T}+{b}^{T})_{2} \\ |\end{aligned}]+⋯+{x}_{m}[\begin{aligned}| \\ ({a}^{T}+{b}^{T})_{m} \\ |\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore, the image of ${R}^{m}$ under the action of ${A}^{T}+{B}^{T}$ must be $\text{Col}({A}^{T}+{B}^{T}),$ the row space of $A+B.$

question.html:
Question 10
?

Let A and B be m×n matrices. What is the image of Rm under the action of AT+BT?

a
Null(AT+BT)
b
Rn
c
Rm
d
Col(AT+BT)
e
0
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, notice that AT+BT is a n×m matrix.

Now, pre-multiplying a vector x∈Rm by AT+BT gives a linear combination of the columns of AT+BT:

[||⋯|(aT+bT)1(aT+bT)2⋯(aT+bT)m||⋯|]⏟AT+BT⋅[x1⋮xm]⏟x=x1[|(aT+bT)1|]+x2[|(aT+bT)2|]+⋯+xm[|(aT+bT)m|]

Therefore, the image of Rm under the action of AT+BT must be Col(AT+BT), the row space of A+B.

question.html:
Question 10
?

Let A and B be m×n matrices. What is the image of Rm under the action of AT+BT?

a
Null(AT+BT)
b
Rn
c
Rm
d
Col(AT+BT)
e
0
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, notice that AT+BT is a n×m matrix.

Now, pre-multiplying a vector x∈Rm by AT+BT gives a linear combination of the columns of AT+BT:

[||⋯|(aT+bT)1(aT+bT)2⋯(aT+bT)m||⋯|]⏟AT+BT⋅[x1⋮xm]⏟x=x1[|(aT+bT)1|]+x2[|(aT+bT)2|]+⋯+xm[|(aT+bT)m|]

Therefore, the image of Rm under the action of AT+BT must be Col(AT+BT), the row space of A+B.
question.knowledge_point: Identifying the Images of the Four Fundamental Subspaces of the Matrix Under Its Action

solution.reasoning: The matrix M=A^T+B^T has size n by m. As x ranges over R^m, Mx ranges over all linear combinations of M's columns, exactly Col(A^T+B^T). Thus option d is correct; the image need not fill R^n. The supplied example supports the general image theorem, but no Math Academy answer or grade for this current question is captured.

feedback.name: Question 10
feedback.problem: Let $A$ and $B$ be $m\times n$ matrices. What is the image of ${R}^{m}$ under the action of ${A}^{T}+{B}^{T}?$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, notice that ${A}^{T}+{B}^{T}$ is a $n\times m$ matrix.

Now, pre-multiplying a vector $x\in {R}^{m}$ by ${A}^{T}+{B}^{T}$ gives a linear combination of the columns of ${A}^{T}+{B}^{T}:$

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}| & | & ⋯ & | \\ ({a}^{T}+{b}^{T})_{1} & ({a}^{T}+{b}^{T})_{2} & ⋯ & ({a}^{T}+{b}^{T})_{m} \\ | & | & ⋯ & |\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{T}+{B}^{T}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{m}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}={x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}| \\ ({a}^{T}+{b}^{T})_{1} \\ |\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}| \\ ({a}^{T}+{b}^{T})_{2} \\ |\end{aligned}]+⋯+{x}_{m}[\begin{aligned}| \\ ({a}^{T}+{b}^{T})_{m} \\ |\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore, the image of ${R}^{m}$ under the action of ${A}^{T}+{B}^{T}$ must be $\text{Col}({A}^{T}+{B}^{T}),$ the row space of $A+B.$

question.name: Question 11
question.problem: Consider a $7\times 8$ matrix $A.$ If $\text{dim}(\text{Col}(A))=4,$ then $\text{dim}(\text{Null}(A))=$
question.worked_solution:
The four fundamental subspaces of a matrix $A$ can be schematically visualized, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14154359/assets/889b83fadd26b377c4dd34143c9b16541630c04e90de3d9b005e7147ead75ad5.png)

In our case, we are given that $m=7,$ $n=8,$ and $r=4.$ 

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{dim}(\text{Null}(A)) & =n-r=8-4=4.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: What is $\sqrt{42}$ rounded to $3$ decimal places?
questions.worked_solution:
Using a calculator, we find that

$$
\sqrt{42}=6.480\,740\,698\,...
$$

Now, we round the value to $3$ decimal places:

$$
\sqrt{42}≈6.481.
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
Which of the following numbers are **NOT** surds?

$$
\sqrt{49},\,\sqrt{28},\,\sqrt{64}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
A surd is a number containing a radical symbol $\sqrt{}$ that cannot be written as a positive or negative whole number or fraction.

With that in mind, let's look at each number in turn.

- $\sqrt{49}$ is **NOT** a surd. Since $49$ is a perfect square, we can get rid of the square root symbol ($\sqrt{}$) and obtain a whole number: 

$$
\sqrt{49}=\sqrt{{7}^{2}}=7
$$

- $\sqrt{28}$ is a surd because $28$ is not a perfect square. In fact $\sqrt{28}=5.291\,502\,622\,...$

- $\sqrt{64}$ is **NOT** a surd. Since $64$ is a perfect square, we can get rid of the square root symbol $(\sqrt{})$ and obtain a whole number:

$$
\sqrt{64}=\sqrt{{8}^{2}}=8
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is: $\sqrt{49}$ and $\sqrt{64}$ only.

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem:
Which of the following numbers are **NOT** surds?

$$
\sqrt{\frac{1}{6}},\,\sqrt{\frac{1}{81}},\,\sqrt{\frac{1}{100}}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
A surd is a number containing a radical symbol $\sqrt{}$ that cannot be written as a positive or negative whole number or fraction.

With that in mind, let's look at each number in turn.

- $\sqrt{\frac{1}{6}}$ is a surd because $\frac{1}{6}$ is not a perfect square. In fact $\sqrt{\frac{1}{6}}=0.408\,248\,…$

- $\sqrt{\frac{1}{81}}$ is **NOT** a surd. Since $1$ and $81$ are perfect squares, we can get rid of the square root symbol $(\sqrt{})$ and obtain a regular fraction.

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{\frac{1}{81}} & =\sqrt{\frac{{1}^{2}}{{9}^{2}}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1\cdot 1}{9\cdot 9}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{9}\cdot \frac{1}{9}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(\frac{1}{9})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\end{aligned}
$$

- $\sqrt{\frac{1}{100}}$ is **NOT** a surd. Since $1$ and $100$ are perfect squares, we can get rid of the square root symbol $(\sqrt{})$ and obtain a regular fraction.

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{\frac{1}{100}} & =\sqrt{\frac{{1}^{2}}{{10}^{2}}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1\cdot 1}{10\cdot 10}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{10}\cdot \frac{1}{10}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(\frac{1}{10})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{10}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is: $\sqrt{\frac{1}{81}}$ and $\sqrt{\frac{1}{100}}$ only.

questions.name: Question 6
questions.problem:
Which of the following numbers are **NOT** surds?

$$
\sqrt{\frac{1}{36}},\,\sqrt{\frac{9}{100}},\,\sqrt{\frac{11}{16}}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
A surd is a number containing a radical symbol $\sqrt{}$ that cannot be written as a positive or negative whole number or fraction.

With that in mind, let's look at each number in turn.

- $\sqrt{\frac{1}{36}}$ is **NOT** a surd. Since $1$ and $36$ are perfect squares, we can get rid of the square root symbol $(\sqrt{})$ and obtain a regular fraction.

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{\frac{1}{36}} & =\sqrt{\frac{{1}^{2}}{{6}^{2}}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1\cdot 1}{6\cdot 6}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{6}\cdot \frac{1}{6}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(\frac{1}{6})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

- $\sqrt{\frac{9}{100}}$ is **NOT** a surd. Since $9$ and $100$ are perfect squares, we can get rid of the square root symbol $(\sqrt{})$ and obtain a regular fraction.

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{\frac{9}{100}} & =\sqrt{\frac{{3}^{2}}{{10}^{2}}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{3\cdot 3}{10\cdot 10}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{3}{10}\cdot \frac{3}{10}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(\frac{3}{10})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3}{10}\end{aligned}
$$

- $\sqrt{\frac{11}{16}}$ is a surd because $\frac{11}{16}$ is not a perfect square. In fact $\sqrt{\frac{11}{16}}=0.829\,156\,…$

Therefore, the correct answer is: $\sqrt{\frac{1}{36}}$ and $\sqrt{\frac{9}{100}}$ only.

questions.name: Question 7
questions.problem:
Which of the following numbers are surds?

$$
\sqrt[3]{10},\,\sqrt[3]{100},\,\sqrt[3]{1\,000}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
A surd is a number containing a radical symbol $\sqrt{}$ that cannot be written as a positive or negative whole number or fraction.

Surds can be square roots $\sqrt{},$ cube roots $\sqrt[3]{},$ or higher roots such as $\sqrt[4]{},$ $\sqrt[5]{},…,$ etc.

With that in mind, let's look at each number in turn.

- $\sqrt[3]{10}$ is a surd because $10$ is not a perfect cube. In fact $\sqrt[3]{10}=2.154\,434\,…$

- $\sqrt[3]{100}$ is a surd because $100$ is not a perfect cube. In fact $\sqrt[3]{100}=4.641\,588\,…$

- $\sqrt[3]{1\,000}$ is **NOT** a surd. Since $1\,000$ is a perfect cube, we can get rid of the cube root symbol $(\sqrt[3]{})$ and obtain a whole number.

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt[3]{1\,000} & =\sqrt[3]{{10}^{3}}=10\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is: $\sqrt[3]{10}$ and $\sqrt[3]{100}$ only.

questions.name: Question 8
questions.problem:
Which of the following numbers are surds?

$$
\sqrt[3]{5},\,\sqrt[3]{50},\,\sqrt[3]{125}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
A surd is a number containing a radical symbol $\sqrt{}$ that cannot be written as a positive or negative whole number or fraction.

Surds can be square roots $\sqrt{},$ cube roots $\sqrt[3]{},$ or higher roots such as $\sqrt[4]{},$ $\sqrt[5]{},…,$ etc.

With that in mind, let's look at each number in turn.

- $\sqrt[3]{5}$ is a surd because $5$ is not a perfect cube. In fact $\sqrt[3]{5}=1.709\,975\,…$

- $\sqrt[3]{50}$ is a surd because $50$ is not a perfect cube. In fact $\sqrt[3]{50}=3.684\,031\,…$

- $\sqrt[3]{125}$ is **NOT** a surd. Since $125$ is a perfect cube, we can get rid of the cube root symbol $(\sqrt[3]{})$ and obtain a whole number.

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt[3]{125} & =\sqrt[3]{{5}^{3}}=5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is: $\sqrt[3]{5}$ and $\sqrt[3]{50}$ only.

canonical_examples.problem:
Which of the following numbers are surds?

$$
\sqrt{2},\qquad \sqrt{8},\qquad \sqrt{16}
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
A surd is a number containing a radical symbol $\sqrt{\phantom{0}}$ that cannot be written as a positive or negative whole number or fraction.

With that in mind, let's look at each number in turn.

- $\sqrt{2}$ is a surd. Using a calculator, we find that $\sqrt{2}=1.414\,213\,562\,...$

- $\sqrt{8}$ is a surd. Using a calculator, we find that $\sqrt{8}=2.828\,427\,124\,...$

- $\sqrt{16}$ is **NOT** a surd. Since $16$ is a perfect square, we can get rid of the square root symbol ($\sqrt{\phantom{x}}$) and obtain a whole number:

$$
\sqrt{16}=\sqrt{4^2}=4
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is: $\sqrt{2}$ and $\sqrt{8}$ only.

canonical_examples.problem:
Which of the following numbers are surds?

$$
\sqrt{\dfrac{5}{12}}, \qquad \sqrt{\dfrac{64}{81}}, \qquad \sqrt{\dfrac{10}{7}}
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
A surd is a number containing a radical symbol $\sqrt{\phantom{0}}$ that cannot be written as a positive or negative whole number or fraction.

With that in mind, let's look at each number in turn.

- $\sqrt{\dfrac{5}{12}}$ is a surd. Using a calculator, we find that $\sqrt{\dfrac{5}{12}} = 0.645\,497\,\ldots$

- $\sqrt{\dfrac{64}{81}}$ is **NOT** a surd. Since $64$ and $81$ are perfect squares, we can get rid of the square root symbol $(\sqrt{\phantom{0}})$ and obtain a regular fraction.

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{\frac{64}{81}} & =\sqrt{\frac{{8}^{2}}{{9}^{2}}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{8\cdot 8}{9\cdot 9}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{8}{9}\cdot \frac{8}{9}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(\frac{8}{9})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{8}{9}\end{aligned}
$$

- $\sqrt{\dfrac{10}{7}}$ is a surd. Using a calculator, we find that $\sqrt{\dfrac{10}{7}} = 1.195\,228\,\ldots$

Therefore, the correct answer is: $\sqrt{\dfrac{5}{12}}$ and $\sqrt{\dfrac{10}{7}}$ only.

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
A surd is a number containing a radical symbol $\sqrt{\phantom{0}}$ that cannot be written as a positive or negative whole number or fraction.

Surds can be square roots $\sqrt{\phantom{0}}$, cube roots $\sqrt[3]{\phantom{0}},$ or higher roots such as $\sqrt[4]{\phantom{0}}, \sqrt[5]{\phantom{0}},\ldots,$ etc.

With that in mind, let's look at each number in turn.

- $\sqrt[3]{2}$ is a surd. Using a calculator, we find that $\sqrt[3]{2} = 1.259\,921\,\ldots$

- $\sqrt[3]{\dfrac{1}{27}}$ is **NOT** a surd. Since $1$ and $27$ are perfect cubes, we can get rid of the cube root symbol $(\sqrt[3]{\phantom{0}})$ and obtain a regular fraction.

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt[3]{\frac{1}{27}} & =\sqrt[3]{\frac{{1}^{3}}{{3}^{3}}} \\  & =\sqrt[3]{\frac{1\cdot 1\cdot 1}{3\cdot 3\cdot 3}} \\  & =\sqrt[3]{\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{1}{3}} \\  & =\sqrt[3]{{(\frac{1}{3})}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

- $\sqrt[3]{11}$ is a surd. Using a calculator, we find that $\sqrt[3]{11} = 2.223\,980\,\ldots$

Therefore, the correct answer is: $\sqrt[3]{2}$ and $\sqrt[3]{11}$ only.

tutorials.name: Numbers That Are Not Surds
tutorials.problem:
A number is *not* a surd if we can write it as a positive or negative whole number or fraction. 

For example, $\sqrt 9$ is *not* a surd because it is a perfect square and can be expressed as a whole number:

$$
\sqrt 9 = \sqrt{3^2} = 3
$$

Similarly, $\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{16}}$ is *not* a surd because it can be written as a regular fraction (i.e., as the ratio of two whole numbers):

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{\frac{1}{16}} & =\sqrt{\frac{1\cdot 1}{4\cdot 4}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{1}{4}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(\frac{1}{4})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we cannot have surds involving square roots of negative numbers. In other words, the numbers 

$$
\sqrt{-2}, \qquad \sqrt{-5}, \qquad \sqrt{-14}
$$

are *not* surds because they are *not real numbers*!

tutorials.name: Surds With Cube Roots
tutorials.problem:
Similarly, we can have surds involving the cube root sign ($\sqrt[3]{\phantom{x}}$). For example, 

$$
\sqrt[3]{2}, \quad\sqrt[3]{9}, \quad \sqrt[3]{11}, \quad \sqrt[3]{129}, \quad \ldots
$$

But $\sqrt[3]{8}$ is **not** a surd since we can get rid of the cube root:

$$
\sqrt[3]{8} = \sqrt[3]{2^3} = 2
$$

Most calculators have a "cube root button" $\bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{\sqrt[3]{\phantom{x}}}$ that can be used to compute cube roots.

Note that we can have surds involving cube roots ($\sqrt[3]{\phantom{x}}$) of negative numbers, such as

$$
\sqrt[3]{-2}, \quad \sqrt[3]{-5}, \quad \sqrt[3]{-14},
$$

because it's fine to take the cube root of a negative number.

\sqrt[3]{-2}, \quad \sqrt[3]{-5}, \quad \sqrt[3]{-14},
$$

because it's fine to take the cube root of a negative number.

tutorial.name: Numbers That Are Not Surds
tutorial.problem:
A number is *not* a surd if we can write it as a positive or negative whole number or fraction. 

For example, $\sqrt 9$ is *not* a surd because it is a perfect square and can be expressed as a whole number:

$$
\sqrt 9 = \sqrt{3^2} = 3
$$

Similarly, $\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{16}}$ is *not* a surd because it can be written as a regular fraction (i.e., as the ratio of two whole numbers):

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{\frac{1}{16}} & =\sqrt{\frac{1\cdot 1}{4\cdot 4}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{1}{4}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(\frac{1}{4})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we cannot have surds involving square roots of negative numbers. In other words, the numbers 

$$
\sqrt{-2}, \qquad \sqrt{-5}, \qquad \sqrt{-14}
$$

are *not* surds because they are *not real numbers*!

observed_steps.worked_solution:
A surd is a number containing a radical symbol $\sqrt{\phantom{0}}$ that cannot be written as a positive or negative whole number or fraction.

With that in mind, let's look at each number in turn.

- $\sqrt{2}$ is a surd. Using a calculator, we find that $\sqrt{2}=1.414\,213\,562\,...$

- $\sqrt{8}$ is a surd. Using a calculator, we find that $\sqrt{8}=2.828\,427\,124\,...$

- $\sqrt{16}$ is **NOT** a surd. Since $16$ is a perfect square, we can get rid of the square root symbol ($\sqrt{\phantom{x}}$) and obtain a whole number:

$$
\sqrt{16}=\sqrt{4^2}=4
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is: $\sqrt{2}$ and $\sqrt{8}$ only.

49 only

49 and 28 only
e
28 and 64 only

Correct

A surd is a number containing a radical symbol 0 that cannot be written as a positive or negative whole number or fraction.

With that in mind, let's look at each number in turn.

  • 49 is NOT a surd. Since 49 is a perfect square, we can get rid of the square root symbol (x) and obtain a whole number: 49=72=7

  • 28 is a surd because 28 is not a perfect square. In fact 28=5.291502622...

  • 64 is NOT a surd. Since 64 is a perfect square, we can get rid of the square root symbol (x) and obtain a whole number: 64=82=8

Therefore, the correct answer is: 49 and 64 only.

question.html:
Question 4
?

Which of the following numbers are surds?

144,25,74

a
74 only
b
74 and 144 only
c
144 and 25 only
d
144 only
e
25 only
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

A surd is a number containing a radical symbol 0 that cannot be written as a positive or negative whole number or fraction.

With that in mind, let's look at each number in turn.

  • 144 is NOT a surd. Since 144 is a perfect square, we can get rid of the square root symbol (x) and obtain a whole number: 144=122=12

  • 25 is NOT a surd. Since 25 is a perfect square, we can get rid of the square root symbol (x) and obtain a whole number: 25=52=5

  • 74 is a surd because 74 is not a perfect square. In fact 74=8.602 325...

Therefore, the correct answer is: 74 only.

A surd is a number containing a radical symbol $\sqrt{\phantom{0}}$ that cannot be written as a positive or negative whole number or fraction.

With that in mind, let's look at each number in turn.

- $\sqrt{\dfrac{5}{12}}$ is a surd. Using a calculator, we find that $\sqrt{\dfrac{5}{12}} = 0.645\,497\,\ldots$

- $\sqrt{\dfrac{64}{81}}$ is **NOT** a surd. Since $64$ and $81$ are perfect squares, we can get rid of the square root symbol $(\sqrt{\phantom{0}})$ and obtain a regular fraction.

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{\frac{64}{81}} & =\sqrt{\frac{{8}^{2}}{{9}^{2}}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{8\cdot 8}{9\cdot 9}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{8}{9}\cdot \frac{8}{9}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(\frac{8}{9})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{8}{9}\end{aligned}
$$

- $\sqrt{\dfrac{10}{7}}$ is a surd. Using a calculator, we find that $\sqrt{\dfrac{10}{7}} = 1.195\,228\,\ldots$

Therefore, the correct answer is: $\sqrt{\dfrac{5}{12}}$ and $\sqrt{\dfrac{10}{7}}$ only.

Question 5
?

Which of the following numbers are NOT surds? 16,181,1100

a
1100 only
b
181 and 1100 only
c
16 only
d
181 only
e
16 and 181 only
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

A surd is a number containing a radical symbol 0 that cannot be written as a positive or negative whole number or fraction.

With that in mind, let's look at each number in turn.

  • 16 is a surd because 16 is not a perfect square. In fact 16=0.408248…

  • 181 is NOT a surd. Since 1 and 81 are perfect squares, we can get rid of the square root symbol (0) and obtain a regular fraction. 181=1292=1⋅19⋅9=19⋅19=(19)2=19

  • 1100 is NOT a surd. Since 1 and 100 are perfect squares, we can get rid of the square root symbol (0) and obtain a regular fraction. 1100=12102=1⋅110⋅10=110⋅110=(110)2=110

Therefore, the correct answer is: 181 and 1100 only.

Question 6

Which of the following numbers are NOT surds? 136,9100,1116

a
9100 and 1116 only
b
1116 only
c
136 and 9100 only
d
9100 only
e
136 only
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

A surd is a number containing a radical symbol 0 that cannot be written as a positive or negative whole number or fraction.

With that in mind, let's look at each number in turn.

  • 136 is NOT a surd. Since 1 and 36 are perfect squares, we can get rid of the square root symbol (0) and obtain a regular fraction. 136=1262=1⋅16⋅6=16⋅16=(16)2=16

  • 9100 is NOT a surd. Since 9 and 100 are perfect squares, we can get rid of the square root symbol (0) and obtain a regular fraction. 9100=32102=3⋅310⋅10=310⋅310=(310)2=310

  • 1116 is a surd because 1116 is not a perfect square. In fact 1116=0.829156…

Therefore, the correct answer is: 136 and 9100 only.

tutorial.name: Surds With Cube Roots
tutorial.problem:
Similarly, we can have surds involving the cube root sign ($\sqrt[3]{\phantom{x}}$). For example, 

$$
\sqrt[3]{2}, \quad\sqrt[3]{9}, \quad \sqrt[3]{11}, \quad \sqrt[3]{129}, \quad \ldots
$$

But $\sqrt[3]{8}$ is **not** a surd since we can get rid of the cube root:

$$
\sqrt[3]{8} = \sqrt[3]{2^3} = 2
$$

Most calculators have a "cube root button" $\bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{\sqrt[3]{\phantom{x}}}$ that can be used to compute cube roots.

Note that we can have surds involving cube roots ($\sqrt[3]{\phantom{x}}$) of negative numbers, such as

$$
\sqrt[3]{-2}, \quad \sqrt[3]{-5}, \quad \sqrt[3]{-14},
$$

because it's fine to take the cube root of a negative number.

question.html:
Question 7
?

Which of the following numbers are surds?

103,1003,10003

a
103 and 10003 only
b
1003 only
c
103 and 1003 only
d
1003 and 10003 only
e
10003 only
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

A surd is a number containing a radical symbol 0 that cannot be written as a positive or negative whole number or fraction.

Surds can be square roots 0, cube roots 03, or higher roots such as 04, 05,…, etc.

With that in mind, let's look at each number in turn.

  • 103 is a surd because 10 is not a perfect cube. In fact 103=2.154434…

  • 1003 is a surd because 100 is not a perfect cube. In fact 1003=4.641588…

  • 10003 is NOT a surd. Since 1000 is a perfect cube, we can get rid of the cube root symbol (03) and obtain a whole number. 10003=1033=10

Therefore, the correct answer is: 103 and 1003 only.

A surd is a number containing a radical symbol $\sqrt{}$ that cannot be written as a positive or negative whole number or fraction.

Surds can be square roots $\sqrt{},$ cube roots $\sqrt[3]{},$ or higher roots such as $\sqrt[4]{},$ $\sqrt[5]{},…,$ etc.

With that in mind, let's look at each number in turn.

- $\sqrt[3]{5}$ is a surd because $5$ is not a perfect cube. In fact $\sqrt[3]{5}=1.709\,975\,…$

- $\sqrt[3]{50}$ is a surd because $50$ is not a perfect cube. In fact $\sqrt[3]{50}=3.684\,031\,…$

- $\sqrt[3]{125}$ is **NOT** a surd. Since $125$ is a perfect cube, we can get rid of the cube root symbol $(\sqrt[3]{})$ and obtain a whole number.

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt[3]{125} & =\sqrt[3]{{5}^{3}}=5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is: $\sqrt[3]{5}$ and $\sqrt[3]{50}$ only.

Introduction
?

We know how to find the square root of a perfect square. But how do we find square roots of numbers that are not perfect squares?

Even though is not a perfect square, is still a number. Such numbers are called surds. Surds are a new type of number that cannot be written as a whole number or regular fraction!

Surds can, however, be written as infinite, non-repeating decimals.

In general, a surd is the th root of a positive rational number, where the result is an irrational number.

question.problem:
Which of the following numbers are **NOT** surds?

$$
\sqrt{49},\,\sqrt{28},\,\sqrt{64}
$$
question.worked_solution:
A surd is a number containing a radical symbol $\sqrt{}$ that cannot be written as a positive or negative whole number or fraction.

With that in mind, let's look at each number in turn.

- $\sqrt{49}$ is **NOT** a surd. Since $49$ is a perfect square, we can get rid of the square root symbol ($\sqrt{}$) and obtain a whole number: 

$$
\sqrt{49}=\sqrt{{7}^{2}}=7
$$

- $\sqrt{28}$ is a surd because $28$ is not a perfect square. In fact $\sqrt{28}=5.291\,502\,622\,...$

- $\sqrt{64}$ is **NOT** a surd. Since $64$ is a perfect square, we can get rid of the square root symbol $(\sqrt{})$ and obtain a whole number:

$$
\sqrt{64}=\sqrt{{8}^{2}}=8
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is: $\sqrt{49}$ and $\sqrt{64}$ only.

question.html:
Question 3
?

Which of the following numbers are NOT surds?

49,28,64

a
64 only
b
49 and 64 only
c
49 only
d
49 and 28 only
e
28 and 64 only
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

A surd is a number containing a radical symbol 0 that cannot be written as a positive or negative whole number or fraction.

With that in mind, let's look at each number in turn.

  • 49 is NOT a surd. Since 49 is a perfect square, we can get rid of the square root symbol (x) and obtain a whole number: 49=72=7

  • 28 is a surd because 28 is not a perfect square. In fact 28=5.291502622...

  • 64 is NOT a surd. Since 64 is a perfect square, we can get rid of the square root symbol (x) and obtain a whole number: 64=82=8

Therefore, the correct answer is: 49 and 64 only.

question.html:
Question 3
?

Which of the following numbers are NOT surds?

49,28,64

a
64 only
b
49 and 64 only
c
49 only
d
49 and 28 only
e
28 and 64 only
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

A surd is a number containing a radical symbol 0 that cannot be written as a positive or negative whole number or fraction.

With that in mind, let's look at each number in turn.

  • 49 is NOT a surd. Since 49 is a perfect square, we can get rid of the square root symbol (x) and obtain a whole number: 49=72=7

  • 28 is a surd because 28 is not a perfect square. In fact 28=5.291502622...

  • 64 is NOT a surd. Since 64 is a perfect square, we can get rid of the square root symbol (x) and obtain a whole number: 64=82=8

Therefore, the correct answer is: 49 and 64 only.

feedback.problem:
Which of the following numbers are **NOT** surds?

$$
\sqrt{49},\,\sqrt{28},\,\sqrt{64}
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
A surd is a number containing a radical symbol $\sqrt{}$ that cannot be written as a positive or negative whole number or fraction.

With that in mind, let's look at each number in turn.

- $\sqrt{49}$ is **NOT** a surd. Since $49$ is a perfect square, we can get rid of the square root symbol ($\sqrt{}$) and obtain a whole number: 

$$
\sqrt{49}=\sqrt{{7}^{2}}=7
$$

- $\sqrt{28}$ is a surd because $28$ is not a perfect square. In fact $\sqrt{28}=5.291\,502\,622\,...$

- $\sqrt{64}$ is **NOT** a surd. Since $64$ is a perfect square, we can get rid of the square root symbol $(\sqrt{})$ and obtain a whole number:

$$
\sqrt{64}=\sqrt{{8}^{2}}=8
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is: $\sqrt{49}$ and $\sqrt{64}$ only.

question.html:
Question 4
?

Which of the following numbers are surds?

144,25,74

a
74 only
b
74 and 144 only
c
144 and 25 only
d
144 only
e
25 only
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

A surd is a number containing a radical symbol 0 that cannot be written as a positive or negative whole number or fraction.

With that in mind, let's look at each number in turn.

  • 144 is NOT a surd. Since 144 is a perfect square, we can get rid of the square root symbol (x) and obtain a whole number: 144=122=12

  • 25 is NOT a surd. Since 25 is a perfect square, we can get rid of the square root symbol (x) and obtain a whole number: 25=52=5

  • 74 is a surd because 74 is not a perfect square. In fact 74=8.602 325...

Therefore, the correct answer is: 74 only.

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
Which of the following numbers are **NOT** surds?

$$
\sqrt{\frac{1}{6}},\,\sqrt{\frac{1}{81}},\,\sqrt{\frac{1}{100}}
$$
question.worked_solution:
A surd is a number containing a radical symbol $\sqrt{}$ that cannot be written as a positive or negative whole number or fraction.

With that in mind, let's look at each number in turn.

- $\sqrt{\frac{1}{6}}$ is a surd because $\frac{1}{6}$ is not a perfect square. In fact $\sqrt{\frac{1}{6}}=0.408\,248\,…$

- $\sqrt{\frac{1}{81}}$ is **NOT** a surd. Since $1$ and $81$ are perfect squares, we can get rid of the square root symbol $(\sqrt{})$ and obtain a regular fraction.

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{\frac{1}{81}} & =\sqrt{\frac{{1}^{2}}{{9}^{2}}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1\cdot 1}{9\cdot 9}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{9}\cdot \frac{1}{9}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(\frac{1}{9})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\end{aligned}
$$

- $\sqrt{\frac{1}{100}}$ is **NOT** a surd. Since $1$ and $100$ are perfect squares, we can get rid of the square root symbol $(\sqrt{})$ and obtain a regular fraction.

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{\frac{1}{100}} & =\sqrt{\frac{{1}^{2}}{{10}^{2}}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1\cdot 1}{10\cdot 10}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{10}\cdot \frac{1}{10}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(\frac{1}{10})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{10}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is: $\sqrt{\frac{1}{81}}$ and $\sqrt{\frac{1}{100}}$ only.

Question 5
?

Which of the following numbers are NOT surds? 16,181,1100

a
1100 only
b
181 and 1100 only
c
16 only
d
181 only
e
16 and 181 only
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

A surd is a number containing a radical symbol 0 that cannot be written as a positive or negative whole number or fraction.

With that in mind, let's look at each number in turn.

  • 16 is a surd because 16 is not a perfect square. In fact 16=0.408248…

  • 181 is NOT a surd. Since 1 and 81 are perfect squares, we can get rid of the square root symbol (0) and obtain a regular fraction. 181=1292=1⋅19⋅9=19⋅19=(19)2=19

  • 1100 is NOT a surd. Since 1 and 100 are perfect squares, we can get rid of the square root symbol (0) and obtain a regular fraction. 1100=12102=1⋅110⋅10=110⋅110=(110)2=110

Therefore, the correct answer is: 181 and 1100 only.

question.html:
Question 5
?

Which of the following numbers are NOT surds? 16,181,1100

a
1100 only
b
181 and 1100 only
c
16 only
d
181 only
e
16 and 181 only
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

A surd is a number containing a radical symbol 0 that cannot be written as a positive or negative whole number or fraction.

With that in mind, let's look at each number in turn.

  • 16 is a surd because 16 is not a perfect square. In fact 16=0.408248…

  • 181 is NOT a surd. Since 1 and 81 are perfect squares, we can get rid of the square root symbol (0) and obtain a regular fraction. 181=1292=1⋅19⋅9=19⋅19=(19)2=19

  • 1100 is NOT a surd. Since 1 and 100 are perfect squares, we can get rid of the square root symbol (0) and obtain a regular fraction. 1100=12102=1⋅110⋅10=110⋅110=(110)2=110

Therefore, the correct answer is: 181 and 1100 only.

feedback.problem:
Which of the following numbers are **NOT** surds?

$$
\sqrt{\frac{1}{6}},\,\sqrt{\frac{1}{81}},\,\sqrt{\frac{1}{100}}
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
A surd is a number containing a radical symbol $\sqrt{}$ that cannot be written as a positive or negative whole number or fraction.

With that in mind, let's look at each number in turn.

- $\sqrt{\frac{1}{6}}$ is a surd because $\frac{1}{6}$ is not a perfect square. In fact $\sqrt{\frac{1}{6}}=0.408\,248\,…$

- $\sqrt{\frac{1}{81}}$ is **NOT** a surd. Since $1$ and $81$ are perfect squares, we can get rid of the square root symbol $(\sqrt{})$ and obtain a regular fraction.

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{\frac{1}{81}} & =\sqrt{\frac{{1}^{2}}{{9}^{2}}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1\cdot 1}{9\cdot 9}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{9}\cdot \frac{1}{9}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(\frac{1}{9})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\end{aligned}
$$

- $\sqrt{\frac{1}{100}}$ is **NOT** a surd. Since $1$ and $100$ are perfect squares, we can get rid of the square root symbol $(\sqrt{})$ and obtain a regular fraction.

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{\frac{1}{100}} & =\sqrt{\frac{{1}^{2}}{{10}^{2}}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1\cdot 1}{10\cdot 10}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{10}\cdot \frac{1}{10}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(\frac{1}{10})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{10}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is: $\sqrt{\frac{1}{81}}$ and $\sqrt{\frac{1}{100}}$ only.

question.problem:
Which of the following numbers are **NOT** surds?

$$
\sqrt{\frac{1}{36}},\,\sqrt{\frac{9}{100}},\,\sqrt{\frac{11}{16}}
$$
question.worked_solution:
A surd is a number containing a radical symbol $\sqrt{}$ that cannot be written as a positive or negative whole number or fraction.

With that in mind, let's look at each number in turn.

- $\sqrt{\frac{1}{36}}$ is **NOT** a surd. Since $1$ and $36$ are perfect squares, we can get rid of the square root symbol $(\sqrt{})$ and obtain a regular fraction.

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{\frac{1}{36}} & =\sqrt{\frac{{1}^{2}}{{6}^{2}}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1\cdot 1}{6\cdot 6}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{6}\cdot \frac{1}{6}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(\frac{1}{6})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

- $\sqrt{\frac{9}{100}}$ is **NOT** a surd. Since $9$ and $100$ are perfect squares, we can get rid of the square root symbol $(\sqrt{})$ and obtain a regular fraction.

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{\frac{9}{100}} & =\sqrt{\frac{{3}^{2}}{{10}^{2}}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{3\cdot 3}{10\cdot 10}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{3}{10}\cdot \frac{3}{10}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(\frac{3}{10})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3}{10}\end{aligned}
$$

- $\sqrt{\frac{11}{16}}$ is a surd because $\frac{11}{16}$ is not a perfect square. In fact $\sqrt{\frac{11}{16}}=0.829\,156\,…$

Therefore, the correct answer is: $\sqrt{\frac{1}{36}}$ and $\sqrt{\frac{9}{100}}$ only.

Question 6

Which of the following numbers are NOT surds? 136,9100,1116

a
9100 and 1116 only
b
1116 only
c
136 and 9100 only
d
9100 only
e
136 only
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

A surd is a number containing a radical symbol 0 that cannot be written as a positive or negative whole number or fraction.

With that in mind, let's look at each number in turn.

  • 136 is NOT a surd. Since 1 and 36 are perfect squares, we can get rid of the square root symbol (0) and obtain a regular fraction. 136=1262=1⋅16⋅6=16⋅16=(16)2=16

  • 9100 is NOT a surd. Since 9 and 100 are perfect squares, we can get rid of the square root symbol (0) and obtain a regular fraction. 9100=32102=3⋅310⋅10=310⋅310=(310)2=310

  • 1116 is a surd because 1116 is not a perfect square. In fact 1116=0.829156…

Therefore, the correct answer is: 136 and 9100 only.

With that in mind, let's look at each number in turn.

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{\frac{1}{36}} & =\sqrt{\frac{{1}^{2}}{{6}^{2}}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1\cdot 1}{6\cdot 6}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{6}\cdot \frac{1}{6}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(\frac{1}{6})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

- $\sqrt{\frac{9}{100}}$ is **NOT** a surd. Since $9$ and $100$ are perfect squares, we can get rid of the square root symbol $(\sqrt{})$ and obtain a regular fraction.

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{\frac{9}{100}} & =\sqrt{\frac{{3}^{2}}{{10}^{2}}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{3\cdot 3}{10\cdot 10}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{3}{10}\cdot \frac{3}{10}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(\frac{3}{10})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3}{10}\end{aligned}
$$

- $\sqrt{\frac{11}{16}}$ is a surd because $\frac{11}{16}$ is not a perfect square. In fact $\sqrt{\frac{11}{16}}=0.829\,156\,…$

Therefore, the correct answer is: $\sqrt{\frac{1}{36}}$ and $\sqrt{\frac{9}{100}}$ only.

question.html:
Question 6
?

Which of the following numbers are NOT surds? 136,9100,1116

a
9100 and 1116 only
b
1116 only
c
136 and 9100 only
d
9100 only
e
136 only
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

A surd is a number containing a radical symbol 0 that cannot be written as a positive or negative whole number or fraction.

With that in mind, let's look at each number in turn.

  • 136 is NOT a surd. Since 1 and 36 are perfect squares, we can get rid of the square root symbol (0) and obtain a regular fraction. 136=1262=1⋅16⋅6=16⋅16=(16)2=16

  • 9100 is NOT a surd. Since 9 and 100 are perfect squares, we can get rid of the square root symbol (0) and obtain a regular fraction. 9100=32102=3⋅310⋅10=310⋅310=(310)2=310

  • 1116 is a surd because 1116 is not a perfect square. In fact 1116=0.829156…

Therefore, the correct answer is: 136 and 9100 only.

solution.reasoning: \sqrt{1/36}=1/6 and \sqrt{9/100}=3/10 are rational, so they are not surds. \sqrt{11/16}=\sqrt{11}/4 is irrational and is a surd. Therefore option c is mathematically correct. No Math Academy answer or grade for this question is captured.

feedback.html:
Question 6
?

Which of the following numbers are NOT surds? 136,9100,1116

a
9100 and 1116 only
b
1116 only
c
136 and 9100 only
d
9100 only
e
136 only
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

A surd is a number containing a radical symbol 0 that cannot be written as a positive or negative whole number or fraction.

With that in mind, let's look at each number in turn.

  • 136 is NOT a surd. Since 1 and 36 are perfect squares, we can get rid of the square root symbol (0) and obtain a regular fraction. 136=1262=1⋅16⋅6=16⋅16=(16)2=16

  • 9100 is NOT a surd. Since 9 and 100 are perfect squares, we can get rid of the square root symbol (0) and obtain a regular fraction. 9100=32102=3⋅310⋅10=310⋅310=(310)2=310

  • 1116 is a surd because 1116 is not a perfect square. In fact 1116=0.829156…

Therefore, the correct answer is: 136 and 9100 only.

question.name: Question 7
question.problem:
Which of the following numbers are surds?

$$
\sqrt[3]{10},\,\sqrt[3]{100},\,\sqrt[3]{1\,000}
$$
question.worked_solution:
A surd is a number containing a radical symbol $\sqrt{}$ that cannot be written as a positive or negative whole number or fraction.

Surds can be square roots $\sqrt{},$ cube roots $\sqrt[3]{},$ or higher roots such as $\sqrt[4]{},$ $\sqrt[5]{},…,$ etc.

With that in mind, let's look at each number in turn.

- $\sqrt[3]{10}$ is a surd because $10$ is not a perfect cube. In fact $\sqrt[3]{10}=2.154\,434\,…$

- $\sqrt[3]{100}$ is a surd because $100$ is not a perfect cube. In fact $\sqrt[3]{100}=4.641\,588\,…$

- $\sqrt[3]{1\,000}$ is **NOT** a surd. Since $1\,000$ is a perfect cube, we can get rid of the cube root symbol $(\sqrt[3]{})$ and obtain a whole number.

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt[3]{1\,000} & =\sqrt[3]{{10}^{3}}=10\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is: $\sqrt[3]{10}$ and $\sqrt[3]{100}$ only.

question.html:
Question 7
?

Which of the following numbers are surds?

103,1003,10003

a
103 and 10003 only
b
1003 only
c
103 and 1003 only
d
1003 and 10003 only
e
10003 only
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

A surd is a number containing a radical symbol 0 that cannot be written as a positive or negative whole number or fraction.

Surds can be square roots 0, cube roots 03, or higher roots such as 04, 05,…, etc.

With that in mind, let's look at each number in turn.

  • 103 is a surd because 10 is not a perfect cube. In fact 103=2.154434…

  • 1003 is a surd because 100 is not a perfect cube. In fact 1003=4.641588…

  • 10003 is NOT a surd. Since 1000 is a perfect cube, we can get rid of the cube root symbol (03) and obtain a whole number. 10003=1033=10

Therefore, the correct answer is: 103 and 1003 only.

last_observation.worked_solution:
A surd is a number containing a radical symbol $\sqrt{}$ that cannot be written as a positive or negative whole number or fraction.

Surds can be square roots $\sqrt{},$ cube roots $\sqrt[3]{},$ or higher roots such as $\sqrt[4]{},$ $\sqrt[5]{},…,$ etc.

With that in mind, let's look at each number in turn.

- $\sqrt[3]{10}$ is a surd because $10$ is not a perfect cube. In fact $\sqrt[3]{10}=2.154\,434\,…$

- $\sqrt[3]{100}$ is a surd because $100$ is not a perfect cube. In fact $\sqrt[3]{100}=4.641\,588\,…$

- $\sqrt[3]{1\,000}$ is **NOT** a surd. Since $1\,000$ is a perfect cube, we can get rid of the cube root symbol $(\sqrt[3]{})$ and obtain a whole number.

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt[3]{1\,000} & =\sqrt[3]{{10}^{3}}=10\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is: $\sqrt[3]{10}$ and $\sqrt[3]{100}$ only.

question.html:
Question 7
?

Which of the following numbers are surds?

103,1003,10003

a
103 and 10003 only
b
1003 only
c
103 and 1003 only
d
1003 and 10003 only
e
10003 only
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

A surd is a number containing a radical symbol 0 that cannot be written as a positive or negative whole number or fraction.

Surds can be square roots 0, cube roots 03, or higher roots such as 04, 05,…, etc.

With that in mind, let's look at each number in turn.

  • 103 is a surd because 10 is not a perfect cube. In fact 103=2.154434…

  • 1003 is a surd because 100 is not a perfect cube. In fact 1003=4.641588…

  • 10003 is NOT a surd. Since 1000 is a perfect cube, we can get rid of the cube root symbol (03) and obtain a whole number. 10003=1033=10

Therefore, the correct answer is: 103 and 1003 only.
question.knowledge_point: Identifying Cube Root Surds

solution.reasoning: 10 and 100 are not perfect cubes, so their cube roots are irrational and are surds. Since 1000=10^3, its cube root is 10 and is not a surd. Thus option c is mathematically correct. The captured example does not establish Math Academy's answer for this question.

Question 7
?

Which of the following numbers are surds?

103,1003,10003

a
103 and 10003 only
b
1003 only
c
103 and 1003 only
d
1003 and 10003 only
e
10003 only
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

A surd is a number containing a radical symbol 0 that cannot be written as a positive or negative whole number or fraction.

Surds can be square roots 0, cube roots 03, or higher roots such as 04, 05,…, etc.

With that in mind, let's look at each number in turn.

  • 103 is a surd because 10 is not a perfect cube. In fact 103=2.154434…

  • 1003 is a surd because 100 is not a perfect cube. In fact 1003=4.641588…

  • 10003 is NOT a surd. Since 1000 is a perfect cube, we can get rid of the cube root symbol (03) and obtain a whole number. 10003=1033=10

Therefore, the correct answer is: 103 and 1003 only.

question.name: Question 8
question.problem:
Which of the following numbers are surds?

$$
\sqrt[3]{5},\,\sqrt[3]{50},\,\sqrt[3]{125}
$$
question.worked_solution:
A surd is a number containing a radical symbol $\sqrt{}$ that cannot be written as a positive or negative whole number or fraction.

Surds can be square roots $\sqrt{},$ cube roots $\sqrt[3]{},$ or higher roots such as $\sqrt[4]{},$ $\sqrt[5]{},…,$ etc.

With that in mind, let's look at each number in turn.

- $\sqrt[3]{5}$ is a surd because $5$ is not a perfect cube. In fact $\sqrt[3]{5}=1.709\,975\,…$

- $\sqrt[3]{50}$ is a surd because $50$ is not a perfect cube. In fact $\sqrt[3]{50}=3.684\,031\,…$

- $\sqrt[3]{125}$ is **NOT** a surd. Since $125$ is a perfect cube, we can get rid of the cube root symbol $(\sqrt[3]{})$ and obtain a whole number.

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt[3]{125} & =\sqrt[3]{{5}^{3}}=5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is: $\sqrt[3]{5}$ and $\sqrt[3]{50}$ only.

last_observation.worked_solution:
A surd is a number containing a radical symbol $\sqrt{}$ that cannot be written as a positive or negative whole number or fraction.

Surds can be square roots $\sqrt{},$ cube roots $\sqrt[3]{},$ or higher roots such as $\sqrt[4]{},$ $\sqrt[5]{},…,$ etc.

With that in mind, let's look at each number in turn.

- $\sqrt[3]{5}$ is a surd because $5$ is not a perfect cube. In fact $\sqrt[3]{5}=1.709\,975\,…$

- $\sqrt[3]{50}$ is a surd because $50$ is not a perfect cube. In fact $\sqrt[3]{50}=3.684\,031\,…$

- $\sqrt[3]{125}$ is **NOT** a surd. Since $125$ is a perfect cube, we can get rid of the cube root symbol $(\sqrt[3]{})$ and obtain a whole number.

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt[3]{125} & =\sqrt[3]{{5}^{3}}=5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is: $\sqrt[3]{5}$ and $\sqrt[3]{50}$ only.

question.html:
Question 8
?

Which of the following numbers are surds?

53,503,1253

a
503 and 1253 only
b
1253 only
c
53 and 503 only
d
53 and 1253 only
e
503 only
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

A surd is a number containing a radical symbol 0 that cannot be written as a positive or negative whole number or fraction.

Surds can be square roots 0, cube roots 03, or higher roots such as 04, 05,…, etc.

With that in mind, let's look at each number in turn.

  • 53 is a surd because 5 is not a perfect cube. In fact 53=1.709975…

  • 503 is a surd because 50 is not a perfect cube. In fact 503=3.684031…

  • 1253 is NOT a surd. Since 125 is a perfect cube, we can get rid of the cube root symbol (03) and obtain a whole number. 1253=533=5

Therefore, the correct answer is: 53 and 503 only.

solution.reasoning: 5 and 50 are not perfect cubes, so their cube roots are irrational and are surds. Since 125=5^3, its cube root is 5 and is not a surd. Therefore option c is mathematically correct. No Math Academy answer or grade for this question is captured.

feedback.html:
Question 8
?

Which of the following numbers are surds?

53,503,1253

a
503 and 1253 only
b
1253 only
c
53 and 503 only
d
53 and 1253 only
e
503 only
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

A surd is a number containing a radical symbol 0 that cannot be written as a positive or negative whole number or fraction.

Surds can be square roots 0, cube roots 03, or higher roots such as 04, 05,…, etc.

With that in mind, let's look at each number in turn.

  • 53 is a surd because 5 is not a perfect cube. In fact 53=1.709975…

  • 503 is a surd because 50 is not a perfect cube. In fact 503=3.684031…

  • 1253 is NOT a surd. Since 125 is a perfect cube, we can get rid of the cube root symbol (03) and obtain a whole number. 1253=533=5

Therefore, the correct answer is: 53 and 503 only.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: Given that $X∼B(5,0.1),$ compute $P(X\le 1).$ Round your final answer to $4$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
For a binomial random variable $X∼B(n,p),$ where $n$ is the number of trials, and $p$ is the probability of success on each trial,  we have the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x}
$$

Here, we have $X∼B(5,0.1),$ so $X$ has the probability mass function

$$
f(x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{x})(0.1)^{x}(0.9)^{5-x}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 1) & =P(X\in \{0,1\}) \\  & =f(0)+f(1) \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{0})(0.1)^{0}(0.9)^{5-0}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{1})(0.1)^{1}(0.9)^{5-1} \\  & =1(0.1)^{0}(0.9)^{5}+5(0.1)(0.9)^{4} \\  & ≈0.9185\end{aligned}
$$

to $4$ decimal places.

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: Given that $X∼B(4,\frac{1}{3}),$ compute $P(X<3).$
questions.worked_solution:
For a binomial random variable $X∼B(n,p),$ where $n$ is the number of trials, and $p$ is the probability of success on each trial,  we have the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x}
$$

Here, we have $X∼B(4,\frac{1}{3}),$ so $X$ has the probability mass function

$$
f(x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{x}){(\frac{1}{3})}^{x}{(\frac{2}{3})}^{4-x}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<3) & =P(X\in \{0,1,2\}) \\  & =f(0)+f(1)+f(2) \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{0}){(\frac{1}{3})}^{0}{(\frac{2}{3})}^{4-0}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{1}){(\frac{1}{3})}^{1}{(\frac{2}{3})}^{4-1}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{2}){(\frac{1}{3})}^{2}{(\frac{2}{3})}^{4-2} \\  & =1{(\frac{1}{3})}^{0}{(\frac{2}{3})}^{4}+4{(\frac{1}{3})}^{1}{(\frac{2}{3})}^{3}+6{(\frac{1}{3})}^{2}{(\frac{2}{3})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{8}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem: Given $X∼B(3,0.4),$ compute $P(0<X\le 2).$
questions.worked_solution:
For a binomial random variable $X∼B(n,p),$ where $n$ is the number of trials, and $p$ is the probability of success on each trial,  we have the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x}
$$

Here, we have $X∼B(3,0.4),$ so $X$ has the probability mass function

$$
f(x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{x})(0.4)^{x}(0.6)^{3-x}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0<X\le 2) & =P(X\in \{1,2\}) \\  & =f(1)+f(2) \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{1})(0.4)^{1}(0.6)^{3-1}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{2})(0.4)^{2}(0.6)^{3-2} \\  & =3(0.4)^{1}(0.6)^{2}+3(0.4)^{2}(0.6)^{1} \\  & =0.72.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem: If $X∼B(6,0.9),$ then, **rounded to $3$ decimal places**, $P(X<5)≈${{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
For a binomial random variable $X∼B(n,p),$ where $n$ is the number of trials, and $p$ is the probability of success on each trial, we have the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x}
$$

Here, we have $X∼B(6,0.9),$ so $X$ has the probability mass function

$$
f(x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{x})(0.9)^{x}(0.1)^{6-x}.
$$

Computing $P(X<5)$ will require us to compute $f(x)$ at $x=0,1,2,3,4.$ However, if we compute the complement $P(X\ge 5)$ instead, then we will only have to compute $f(x)$ at $x=5,6,$ which will result in a much faster computation.

Computing $P(X\ge 5),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\ge 5) & =P(X\in \{5,6\}) \\  & =f(5)+f(6) \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{5})(0.9)^{5}(0.1)^{6-5}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{6})(0.9)^{6}(0.1)^{6-6} \\  & =6(0.9)^{5}(0.1)+(0.9)^{6} \\  & ≈0.886\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<5) & =1-P(X\ge 5) \\  & ≈1-0.886 \\  & ≈0.114\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\ge 2) & =1-P(X<2) \\  & ≈1-0.016 \\  & =0.984\end{aligned}

$$

Therefore, we have

$$
