question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 1 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}]
$$

The vectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are eigenvectors that correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=3$ of the matrix $A,$ given above. Find the third eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[a,\,b,\,c]^{T}$ such that the set $\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\}$ is linearly independent. What is the value of $\frac{a}{c}?$
question.worked_solution:
First, we find all the eigenvalues of $A$ by solving the characteristic equation $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 1-\lambda  & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & -2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-2-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-2-\lambda )((1-\lambda )(1-\lambda )-(2)(2)) & =0 \\ (-2-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda -3) & =0 \\ (\lambda +2)(\lambda +1)(\lambda -3) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, ${\lambda }_{1}=-1,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=3,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=-2.$ Since we obtained three distinct eigenvalues, the set of eigenvectors $\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\},$ where each vector corresponds to different eigenvalue, will be linearly independent.

Now, recall that ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=3.$ Thus, the third eigenvector ${v}_{3}$ must correspond to ${\lambda }_{3}=-2.$ 

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =-2.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 1 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}]-(-2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 3 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}3{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}+4{x}_{3}=0 \\ 2{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}-4{x}_{3}=0 \\ 0=0\end{aligned}
$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & 4 & 0 \\ 2 & 3 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-\frac{2}{3}){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{5}{3} & -\frac{20}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=4{x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =\frac{1}{3}(-2{x}_{2}-4{x}_{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(-2(4{x}_{3})-4{x}_{3}) \\  & =-4{x}_{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-4{x}_{3} \\ 4{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{3}=1,$ we get the following eigenvector:

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 4 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{c}=\frac{-4}{1}=-4.$

\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 1-\lambda  & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & -2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-2-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-2-\lambda )((1-\lambda )(1-\lambda )-(2)(2)) & =0 \\ (-2-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda -3) & =0 \\ (\lambda +2)(\lambda +1)(\lambda -3) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, ${\lambda }_{1}=-1,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=3,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=-2.$ Since we obtained three distinct eigenvalues, the set of eigenvectors $\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\},$ where each vector corresponds to different eigenvalue, will be linearly independent.

Now, recall that ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=3.$ Thus, the third eigenvector ${v}_{3}$ must correspond to ${\lambda }_{3}=-2.$ 

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =-2.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 1 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}]-(-2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 3 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}3{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}+4{x}_{3}=0 \\ 2{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}-4{x}_{3}=0 \\ 0=0\end{aligned}
$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & 4 & 0 \\ 2 & 3 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-\frac{2}{3}){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{5}{3} & -\frac{20}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=4{x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =\frac{1}{3}(-2{x}_{2}-4{x}_{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(-2(4{x}_{3})-4{x}_{3}) \\  & =-4{x}_{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-4{x}_{3} \\ 4{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{3}=1,$ we get the following eigenvector:

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 4 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{c}=\frac{-4}{1}=-4.$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
Find an eigenvector of $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -2 \\ 0 & 5 & -4 \\ 0 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}]$
that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =3.$
question.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =3.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -2 \\ 0 & 5 & -4 \\ 0 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & -4 \\ 0 & 2 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}=0 \\ 2{x}_{2}-4{x}_{3}=0 \\ 2{x}_{2}-4{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=2{x}_{3}.$ Substituting this in the first equation, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =\frac{1}{2}(2{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(4{x}_{3}-2{x}_{3}) \\  & ={x}_{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{3} \\ 2{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{3}=1,$ we get the eigenvector
$v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

question.html:
Question 4
?

Find an eigenvector of A=[12−205−402−1] that corresponds to the eigenvalue λ=3.

a
[100]
b
[122]
c
[221]
d
[121]
e
[011]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation (A−λI)x=0.

In our case, we have λ=3. So, we obtain

A−λI=[12−205−402−1]−3[100010001]=[−22−202−402−4].

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

{−2x1+2x2−2x3=02x2−4x3=02x2−4x3=0

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix M to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

M=[−22−2002−4002−40]R3:=R3+(−1)R2∼[−22−2002−400000]

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the 1st and the 2nd). Thus, x3 is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain x2=2x3. Substituting this in the first equation, we get x1=12(2x2−2x3)=12(4x3−2x3)=x3.

Therefore, the general solution is [x32x3x3],x3∈R.

Setting, for instance, x3=1, we get the eigenvector v=[121].

last_observation.name: Question 4
last_observation.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =3.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -2 \\ 0 & 5 & -4 \\ 0 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & -4 \\ 0 & 2 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}=0 \\ 2{x}_{2}-4{x}_{3}=0 \\ 2{x}_{2}-4{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=2{x}_{3}.$ Substituting this in the first equation, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =\frac{1}{2}(2{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(4{x}_{3}-2{x}_{3}) \\  & ={x}_{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{3} \\ 2{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{3}=1,$ we get the eigenvector
$v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

feedback.name: Question 4
feedback.problem:
Find an eigenvector of $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -2 \\ 0 & 5 & -4 \\ 0 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}]$
that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =3.$
feedback.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =3.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -2 \\ 0 & 5 & -4 \\ 0 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & -4 \\ 0 & 2 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}=0 \\ 2{x}_{2}-4{x}_{3}=0 \\ 2{x}_{2}-4{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=2{x}_{3}.$ Substituting this in the first equation, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =\frac{1}{2}(2{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(4{x}_{3}-2{x}_{3}) \\  & ={x}_{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{3} \\ 2{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{3}=1,$ we get the eigenvector
$v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 & -4 \\ 3 & -3 & -3 \\ -4 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

The vectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are eigenvectors that correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-3$ of the matrix $A,$ given above. Find the third eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[a,\,b,\,c]^{T}$ such that the set $\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\}$ is linearly independent. What is the value of $\frac{a}{b}?$
question.worked_solution:
First, we find all the eigenvalues of $A$ by solving the characteristic equation $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-4-\lambda  & 0 & -4 \\ 3 & -3-\lambda  & -3 \\ -4 & 0 & 2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-3-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}-4-\lambda  & -4 \\ -4 & 2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-3-\lambda )((-4-\lambda )(2-\lambda )-(-4)(-4)) & =0 \\ (-3-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda -24) & =0 \\ (\lambda +3)(\lambda +6)(\lambda -4) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, ${\lambda }_{1}=4,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-3,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=-6.$ Since we obtained three distinct eigenvalues, the set of eigenvectors $\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\},$ where each vector corresponds to different eigenvalue, will be linearly independent.

Now, recall that ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-3.$ Thus, the third eigenvector ${v}_{3}$ must correspond to ${\lambda }_{3}=-6.$ 

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =-6.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 & -4 \\ 3 & -3 & -3 \\ -4 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]-(-6)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -4 \\ 3 & 3 & -3 \\ -4 & 0 & 8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-4{x}_{3}=0 \\ 3{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}-3{x}_{3}=0 \\ -4{x}_{1}+8{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -4 & 0 \\ 3 & 3 & -3 & 0 \\ -4 & 0 & 8 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 3 & 0 \\ -4 & 0 & 8 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+4{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=-{x}_{3}.$ From the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=2{x}_{3}.$
Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{3} \\ -{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{3}=1,$ we get the following eigenvector:

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{2}{-1}=-2.$

last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we find all the eigenvalues of $A$ by solving the characteristic equation $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-4-\lambda  & 0 & -4 \\ 3 & -3-\lambda  & -3 \\ -4 & 0 & 2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-3-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}-4-\lambda  & -4 \\ -4 & 2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-3-\lambda )((-4-\lambda )(2-\lambda )-(-4)(-4)) & =0 \\ (-3-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda -24) & =0 \\ (\lambda +3)(\lambda +6)(\lambda -4) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, ${\lambda }_{1}=4,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-3,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=-6.$ Since we obtained three distinct eigenvalues, the set of eigenvectors $\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\},$ where each vector corresponds to different eigenvalue, will be linearly independent.

Now, recall that ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-3.$ Thus, the third eigenvector ${v}_{3}$ must correspond to ${\lambda }_{3}=-6.$ 

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =-6.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 & -4 \\ 3 & -3 & -3 \\ -4 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]-(-6)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -4 \\ 3 & 3 & -3 \\ -4 & 0 & 8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-4{x}_{3}=0 \\ 3{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}-3{x}_{3}=0 \\ -4{x}_{1}+8{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -4 & 0 \\ 3 & 3 & -3 & 0 \\ -4 & 0 & 8 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 3 & 0 \\ -4 & 0 & 8 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+4{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=-{x}_{3}.$ From the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=2{x}_{3}.$
Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{3} \\ -{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{3}=1,$ we get the following eigenvector:

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{2}{-1}=-2.$

Hence, λ1=4, λ2=−3, and λ3=−6. Since we obtained three distinct eigenvalues, the set of eigenvectors {v1,v2,v3}, where each vector corresponds to different eigenvalue, will be linearly independent.

Now, recall that v1 and v2 correspond to the eigenvalues λ1=4 and λ2=−3. Thus, the third eigenvector v3 must correspond to λ3=−6.

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation (A−λI)x=0.

In our case, we have λ=−6. So, we obtain

A−λI=[−40−43−3−3−402]−(−6)[100010001]=[20−433−3−408].

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

{2x1−4x3=03x1+3x2−3x3=0−4x1+8x3=0

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix M to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

M=[20−4033−30−4080]R1:=12R1R2:=R2+(−3)R1∼[10−200330−4080]R3:=R3+4R1∼[10−2003300000].

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the 1st and the 2nd). Thus, x3 is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain x2=−x3. From the first equation, we get x1=2x3. Therefore, the general solution is [2x3−x3x3],x3∈R.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: Given that $\{i,j,k\}$ is the standard basis of ${R}^{3}$ and that the images of $i,$ $j,$ and $k$ under the action of a linear transformation $T$ are $⟨2,-1,6⟩,$ $⟨7,2,0⟩,$ and $⟨1,-4,6⟩,$ respectively, what is the standard matrix of $T?$
questions.worked_solution:
Every linear transformation in ${R}^{3}$ can be represented as a $3\times 3$ matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors $i,j,$ and $k$ under the action of the transformation.

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is 

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}2 & 7 & 1 \\ -1 & 2 & -4 \\ 6 & 0 & 6\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.raw_html:
1.?

Given that {i,j,k} is the standard basis of R3 and that the images of i, j, and k under the action of a linear transformation T are ⟨2,−1,6⟩, ⟨7,2,0⟩, and ⟨1,−4,6⟩, respectively, what is the standard matrix of T?

M
Mon, Oct 12th @ 6:07 PM|Elapsed: 0:17Correct

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: Given that $\{i,j\}$ is the standard basis of ${R}^{2}$ and that the images of $i$ and $j$ under the action of a linear transformation $T$ are $⟨1,-1⟩$ and $⟨2,3⟩$, respectively, what is the standard matrix of $T?$
questions.worked_solution:
Every linear transformation in ${R}^{2}$ can be represented as a $2\times 2$ matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors $i$ and $j$ under the action of the transformation.

Therefore, the standard matrix for this linear transformation is 

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem: Given that $\{i,j,k\}$ is the standard basis of ${R}^{3}$ and that the images of $i,$ $j,$ and $k$ under the action of a linear transformation $T$ are $⟨6,2,0⟩,$ $⟨-3,5,6⟩,$ and $⟨-1,2,7⟩,$ respectively, what is the standard matrix of $T?$
questions.worked_solution:
Every linear transformation in ${R}^{3}$ can be represented as a $3\times 3$ matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors $i,j,$ and $k$ under the action of the transformation.

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is 

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}6 & -3 & -1 \\ 2 & 5 & 2 \\ 0 & 6 & 7\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.raw_html:
4.?

Given that {i,j,k} is the standard basis of R3 and that the images of i, j, and k under the action of a linear transformation T are ⟨6,2,0⟩, ⟨−3,5,6⟩, and ⟨−1,2,7⟩, respectively, what is the standard matrix of T?

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem: Given that $\{i,j\}$ is the standard basis of ${R}^{2}$ and that the images of $i$ and $j$ under the action of a linear transformation $T$ are $⟨1,4⟩$ and $⟨5,-1⟩$, respectively, what is the standard matrix of $T?$
questions.worked_solution:
Every linear transformation in ${R}^{2}$ can be represented as a $2\times 2$ matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors $i$ and $j$ under the action of the transformation.

Therefore, the standard matrix for this linear transformation is 

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}1 & 5 \\ 4 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

5.?

Given that {i,j} is the standard basis of R2 and that the images of i and j under the action of a linear transformation T are ⟨1,4⟩ and ⟨5,−1⟩, respectively, what is the standard matrix of T?

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14154685/assets/09423b097ab02b339f15af831e0e35f59ff88cb00c0ef72d3693ce9f24e6b9dc.png)

In the diagram above, $i$ and $j$ are the vectors of the standard basis of ${R}^{2}$, while ${i}^{′}$ and ${j}^{′}$ are their images under the linear transformation $T.$
What is the standard matrix of $T?$
questions.worked_solution:
Every linear transformation in ${R}^{2}$ can be represented as a $2\times 2$ matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors $i$ and $j$ under the action of the transformation.

From the diagram we see that 
${i}^{′}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -3\end{aligned}]$ 
and 
${j}^{′}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is 

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ -3 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14154685/assets/ad1f032fd5b99252d348d0cf71308ef1de0f65f06ddd9070b569cff69bc506f9.png)

In the diagram above, $i$ and $j$ are the vectors of the standard basis of ${R}^{2}$, while ${i}^{′}$ and ${j}^{′}$ are their images under the linear transformation $T.$
What is the standard matrix of $T?$
questions.worked_solution:
Every linear transformation in ${R}^{2}$ can be represented as a $2\times 2$ matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors $i$ and $j$ under the action of the transformation.

From the diagram we see that 
${i}^{′}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ 
and 
${j}^{′}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is 

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14154685/assets/20aff9b0dd1ea6aaab8cfa932317e83015956ac355349d5ae3d744de289bdae5.png)

In the diagram above, $i$ and $j$ are the vectors of the standard basis of ${R}^{2}$, while ${i}^{′}$ and ${j}^{′}$ are their images under the linear transformation $T.$
What is the standard matrix of $T?$
questions.worked_solution:
Every linear transformation in ${R}^{2}$ can be represented as a $2\times 2$ matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors $i$ and $j$ under the action of the transformation.

From the diagram we see that 
${i}^{′}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ 
and 
${j}^{′}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is 

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.name: Question 11
questions.problem:
The linear transformation $T$ has the standard matrix 

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ -7 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

 
What are the respective images of the standard basis vectors $\{i,j\}$ of ${R}^{2}$ under the action of $T?$
questions.worked_solution:
**Method 1**

The images of the vectors in the standard basis $\{i,j\}$ are the first and second columns of $T,$ respectively. 

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(i) & =T[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -7\end{aligned}] \\ T(j) & =T[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

**Method 2**

We can find the images of the vectors in the standard basis $\{i,j\}$ by computing the matrix products $T\cdot i$ and $T\cdot j:$

$$
\begin{aligned}T(i) & =T\cdot i=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ -7 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -7\end{aligned}] \\ T(j) & =T\cdot j=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ -7 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 12
questions.problem:
The linear transformation $T$ has the standard matrix 

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}5 & -2 & 3 \\ 4 & 1 & -5 \\ 8 & -1 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

What are the respective images of the standard basis vectors $\{i,j,k\}$ of ${R}^{3}$ under the action of $T?$
questions.worked_solution:
**Method 1**

The images of the vectors in the standard basis $\{i,j,k\}$ are the first, second, and third columns of $T,$ respectively. 

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(i) & =T[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 4 \\ 8\end{aligned}] \\ T(j) & =T[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\ T(k) & =T[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -5 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

**Method 2**

We can find the images of the vectors in the standard basis $\{i,j,k\}$ by computing the matrix products $T\cdot i,$ $T\cdot j,$ and $T\cdot k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}T(i) & =T\cdot i=[\begin{aligned}5 & -2 & 3 \\ 4 & 1 & -5 \\ 8 & -1 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 4 \\ 8\end{aligned}] \\ T(j) & =T\cdot j=[\begin{aligned}5 & -2 & 3 \\ 4 & 1 & -5 \\ 8 & -1 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\ T(k) & =T\cdot k=[\begin{aligned}5 & -2 & 3 \\ 4 & 1 & -5 \\ 8 & -1 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -5 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 13
questions.problem:
The linear transformation $T$ has the standard matrix 

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}4 & -4 \\ 5 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

 
What are the respective images of the standard basis vectors $\{i,j\}$ of ${R}^{2}$ under the action of $T?$
questions.worked_solution:
**Method 1**

The images of the vectors in the standard basis $\{i,j\}$ are the first and second columns of $T,$ respectively. 

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(i) & =T[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\ T(j) & =T[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

**Method 2**

We can find the images of the vectors in the standard basis $\{i,j\}$ by computing the matrix products $T\cdot i$ and $T\cdot j:$

$$
\begin{aligned}T(i) & =T\cdot i=[\begin{aligned}4 & -4 \\ 5 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\ T(j) & =T\cdot j=[\begin{aligned}4 & -4 \\ 5 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
The linear transformation $T$ has the standard matrix 

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 & -1 \\ -3 & 5 & -2 \\ 0 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

What are the respective images of the standard basis vectors $\{i,j,k\}$ of ${R}^{3}$ under the action of $T?$
questions.worked_solution:
**Method 1**

The images of the vectors in the standard basis $\{i,j,k\}$ are the first, second, and third columns of $T,$ respectively. 

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(i) & =T[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ T(j) & =T[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 5 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\ T(k) & =T[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

**Method 2**

We can find the images of the vectors in the standard basis $\{i,j,k\}$ by computing the matrix products $T\cdot i,$ $T\cdot j,$ and $T\cdot k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}T(i) & =T\cdot i=[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 & -1 \\ -3 & 5 & -2 \\ 0 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ T(j) & =T\cdot j=[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 & -1 \\ -3 & 5 & -2 \\ 0 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 5 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\ T(k) & =T\cdot k=[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 & -1 \\ -3 & 5 & -2 \\ 0 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 15
questions.problem:
The linear transformation $T$ has the standard matrix 

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 \\ 4 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

What are the respective images of the standard basis vectors $\{i,j,k\}$ of ${R}^{3}$ under the action of $T?$
questions.worked_solution:
**Method 1**

The images of the vectors in the standard basis $\{i,j,k\}$ are the first, second, and third columns of $T,$ respectively. 

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(i) & =T[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ T(j) & =T[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ T(k) & =T[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

**Method 2**

We can find the images of the vectors in the standard basis $\{i,j,k\}$ by computing the matrix products $T\cdot i,$ $T\cdot j,$ and $T\cdot k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}T(i) & =T\cdot i=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 \\ 4 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ T(j) & =T\cdot j=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 \\ 4 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ T(k) & =T\cdot k=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 \\ 4 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Determining the Standard Matrix of a Linear Transformation Given the Image of the Standard Basis
canonical_examples.problem:
Given that $\{ \mathbf{i}, \mathbf{j}, \mathbf k\}$ is the standard basis of $\mathbb{R}^3$ and the images of $\mathbf{i},$ $\mathbf{j},$ and $\mathbf{k}$ under the action of a linear transformation $\mathbf{T}$ are
$\langle 3, 5, -1 \rangle,$ $\langle 0, 4,3 \rangle,$ and $\langle -1, 5, -2\rangle,$ respectively, what is the standard matrix of $\mathbf{T}?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Every linear transformation in $\mathbb{R}^3$ can be represented as a $3\times 3$ matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors $\mathbf{i}, \mathbf{j},$ and $\mathbf k$ under the action of the transformation.

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is

Example: 
                    Determining the Images of the Standard Basis Vectors Under a Given Linear Transformation
canonical_examples.problem:
The linear transformation $\mathbf T$ has the standard matrix 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14154685/assets/6a14933078db8802426a1ab22ba692e17fd6f795ec4bd746a6fb16687aa441ed.svg) 
What are the images of the standard basis vectors $\{ \mathbf{i}, \mathbf{j} \}$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$ under the action of $\mathbf T?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
**Method 1**

The images of the vectors in the standard basis $\{ \mathbf{i}, \mathbf{j} \}$ are the first and second columns of $T,$ respectively. 

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(i) & =T[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 8\end{aligned}] \\ T(j) & =T[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

**Method 2**

We can find the images of the vectors in the standard basis $\{ \mathbf{i}, \mathbf{j} \}$ by computing the matrix products $T\cdot\mathbf{i}$ and $T\cdot\mathbf{j}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(i) & =T\cdot i=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 5 \\ 8 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 8\end{aligned}] \\ T(j) & =T\cdot j=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 5 \\ 8 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Determining the Images of the Standard Basis Vectors Under a Given Linear Transformation

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
To construct the standard matrix of a linear transformation $T$ in $\mathbb{R}^2,$ we find the images of the vectors in the standard basis $\{ \mathbf{i}, \mathbf{j} \}$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$ under $T,$ and then use those images as columns in the standard matrix.

To demonstrate, let's consider the following linear transformation: 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14154685/assets/b399f02949935d4a4425b19e4946a3eb47375272bb0271586c93da504ff0bd2e.svg)

Computing $\mathbf T(\mathbf i),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}T(i) & =T[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\cdot 1-1\cdot 0 \\ 1+3\cdot 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $\mathbf T(\mathbf j),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}T(j) & =T[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\cdot 0-1\cdot 1 \\ 0+3\cdot 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the standard matrix for this linear transformation is ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14154685/assets/be0afb6703a6d5e4bcbb360297240a74f4aeec7efbbb1229c8cd01e112fa6bda.svg)

In the diagram below, we see the vectors in the standard basis $\{ \mathbf{i}, \mathbf{j} \}$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$ and their images $\{ \mathbf{i'}, \mathbf{j'} \}$ under the transformation.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14154685/assets/9189a79fe44936221e38e7c051f9f0ddd53338c80cd324ba804d61beef6c2c44.png)

In general, a linear transformation in $\mathbb R^n$ has a standard matrix of dimensions $n \times n,$ whose columns are the images of the basis vectors under the action of the linear transformation.

tutorials.content:
To construct the standard matrix of a linear transformation $T$ in $\mathbb{R}^2,$ we find the images of the vectors in the standard basis $\{ \mathbf{i}, \mathbf{j} \}$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$ under $T,$ and then use those images as columns in the standard matrix.

To demonstrate, let's consider the following linear transformation: 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14154685/assets/b399f02949935d4a4425b19e4946a3eb47375272bb0271586c93da504ff0bd2e.svg)

Computing $\mathbf T(\mathbf i),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}T(i) & =T[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\cdot 1-1\cdot 0 \\ 1+3\cdot 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $\mathbf T(\mathbf j),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}T(j) & =T[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\cdot 0-1\cdot 1 \\ 0+3\cdot 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the standard matrix for this linear transformation is ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14154685/assets/be0afb6703a6d5e4bcbb360297240a74f4aeec7efbbb1229c8cd01e112fa6bda.svg)

In the diagram below, we see the vectors in the standard basis $\{ \mathbf{i}, \mathbf{j} \}$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$ and their images $\{ \mathbf{i'}, \mathbf{j'} \}$ under the transformation.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14154685/assets/9189a79fe44936221e38e7c051f9f0ddd53338c80cd324ba804d61beef6c2c44.png)

In general, a linear transformation in $\mathbb R^n$ has a standard matrix of dimensions $n \times n,$ whose columns are the images of the basis vectors under the action of the linear transformation.

tutorial.content:
To construct the standard matrix of a linear transformation $T$ in $\mathbb{R}^2,$ we find the images of the vectors in the standard basis $\{ \mathbf{i}, \mathbf{j} \}$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$ under $T,$ and then use those images as columns in the standard matrix.

To demonstrate, let's consider the following linear transformation: 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14154685/assets/ff83f844bbeb50d9404bdd069e0626d448181a6eb8547b8e27af5da577fa46ec.svg)

Computing $\mathbf T(\mathbf i),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}T(i) & =T[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\cdot 1-1\cdot 0 \\ 1+3\cdot 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $\mathbf T(\mathbf j),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}T(j) & =T[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\cdot 0-1\cdot 1 \\ 0+3\cdot 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the standard matrix for this linear transformation is ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14154685/assets/a3254321a9703ee10ff3dd9bd33cf9511e84abd65fe4ddab7908367c7f7669ac.svg)

In the diagram below, we see the vectors in the standard basis $\{ \mathbf{i}, \mathbf{j} \}$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$ and their images $\{ \mathbf{i'}, \mathbf{j'} \}$ under the transformation.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14154685/assets/9189a79fe44936221e38e7c051f9f0ddd53338c80cd324ba804d61beef6c2c44.png)

In general, a linear transformation in $\mathbb R^n$ has a standard matrix of dimensions $n \times n,$ whose columns are the images of the basis vectors under the action of the linear transformation.

question.problem:
Given that $\{ \mathbf{i}, \mathbf{j}, \mathbf k\}$ is the standard basis of $\mathbb{R}^3$ and the images of $\mathbf{i},$ $\mathbf{j},$ and $\mathbf{k}$ under the action of a linear transformation $\mathbf{T}$ are
$\langle 3, 5, -1 \rangle,$ $\langle 0, 4,3 \rangle,$ and $\langle -1, 5, -2\rangle,$ respectively, what is the standard matrix of $\mathbf{T}?$

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Determining the Standard Matrix of a Linear Transformation Given the Image of the Standard Basis

browser_events.message: Failed to load resource: the server responded with a status of 502 ()

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Every linear transformation in ${R}^{3}$ can be represented as a $3\times 3$ matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors $i,j,$ and $k$ under the action of the transformation.

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is 

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}2 & 7 & 1 \\ -1 & 2 & -4 \\ 6 & 0 & 6\end{aligned}].
$$

question.name: Question 1
question.problem: Given that $\{i,j,k\}$ is the standard basis of ${R}^{3}$ and that the images of $i,$ $j,$ and $k$ under the action of a linear transformation $T$ are $⟨2,-1,6⟩,$ $⟨7,2,0⟩,$ and $⟨1,-4,6⟩,$ respectively, what is the standard matrix of $T?$
question.worked_solution:
Every linear transformation in ${R}^{3}$ can be represented as a $3\times 3$ matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors $i,j,$ and $k$ under the action of the transformation.

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is 

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}2 & 7 & 1 \\ -1 & 2 & -4 \\ 6 & 0 & 6\end{aligned}].
$$

Question 1
?

Given that {i,j,k} is the standard basis of R3 and that the images of i, j, and k under the action of a linear transformation T are ⟨2,−1,6⟩, ⟨7,2,0⟩, and ⟨1,−4,6⟩, respectively, what is the standard matrix of T?

a
 [271−142606]
b
 [271−12−4606]
c
 [2−167201−46]
d
 [271−124606]
e
 [217−1−42660]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Every linear transformation in R3 can be represented as a 3×3 matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors i,j, and k under the action of the transformation.

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is T=[271−12−4606].

question.html:
Question 3
?

Given that {i,j} is the standard basis of R2 and that the images of i and j under the action of a linear transformation T are ⟨2,4⟩ and ⟨1,−5⟩, respectively, what is the standard matrix of T?

a
 [2451]
b
 [214−5]
c
 [2−145]
d
 [241−5]
e
 [12−54]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Every linear transformation in R2 can be represented as a 2×2 matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors i and j under the action of the transformation.

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is
T=[214−5].

question.problem: Given that $\{i,j,k\}$ is the standard basis of ${R}^{3}$ and that the images of $i,$ $j,$ and $k$ under the action of a linear transformation $T$ are $⟨6,2,0⟩,$ $⟨-3,5,6⟩,$ and $⟨-1,2,7⟩,$ respectively, what is the standard matrix of $T?$
question.worked_solution:
Every linear transformation in ${R}^{3}$ can be represented as a $3\times 3$ matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors $i,j,$ and $k$ under the action of the transformation.

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is 

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}6 & -3 & -1 \\ 2 & 5 & 2 \\ 0 & 6 & 7\end{aligned}].
$$

question.html:
Question 4
?

Given that {i,j,k} is the standard basis of R3 and that the images of i, j, and k under the action of a linear transformation T are ⟨6,2,0⟩, ⟨−3,5,6⟩, and ⟨−1,2,7⟩, respectively, what is the standard matrix of T?

a
[6−3−1252067]
b
[0672526−3−1]
c
[0676−3−1252]
d
[620−356−127]
e
[−127−356620]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Every linear transformation in R3 can be represented as a 3×3 matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors i,j, and k under the action of the transformation.

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is T=[6−3−1252067].

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Every linear transformation in ${R}^{2}$ can be represented as a $2\times 2$ matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors $i$ and $j$ under the action of the transformation.

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}1 & 5 \\ 4 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Question 5
?

Given that {i,j} is the standard basis of R2 and that the images of i and j under the action of a linear transformation T are ⟨1,4⟩ and ⟨5,−1⟩, respectively, what is the standard matrix of T?

a
 [1451]
b
 [−1541]
c
 [154−1]
d
 [15−41]
e
 [145−1]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Every linear transformation in R2 can be represented as a 2×2 matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors i and j under the action of the transformation.

Therefore, the standard matrix for this linear transformation is T=[154−1].

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Every linear transformation in ${R}^{2}$ can be represented as a $2\times 2$ matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors $i$ and $j$ under the action of the transformation.

From the diagram we see that 
${i}^{′}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -3\end{aligned}]$ 
and 
${j}^{′}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is 

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ -3 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Question 6
?

In the diagram above, i and j are the vectors of the standard basis of R2, while i′ and j′ are their images under the linear transformation T. What is the standard matrix of T?

a
[13−2−3]
b
[1−2−33]
c
[1−23−3]
d
[−2−313]
e
[−21−33]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Every linear transformation in R2 can be represented as a 2×2 matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors i and j under the action of the transformation.

From the diagram we see that i′=[−2−3] and j′=[13].

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is

T=[−21−33].

Question 7
?

In the diagram above, i and j are the vectors of the standard basis of R2, while i′ and j′ are their images under the linear transformation T. What is the standard matrix of T?

a
[−2231]
b
 [21−23]
c
 [−2123]
d
 [2−213]
e
 [−2321]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Every linear transformation in R2 can be represented as a 2×2 matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors i and j under the action of the transformation.

From the diagram we see that i′=[−23] and j′=[21].

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is

T=[−2231].

question.html:
Question 8
?

In the diagram above, i and j are the vectors of the standard basis of R2, while i′ and j′ are their images under the linear transformation T. What is the standard matrix of T?

a
 [112−1]
b
[1−12−1]
c
[−121−1]
d
 [−1−112]
e
 [12−1−1]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Every linear transformation in R2 can be represented as a 2×2 matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors i and j under the action of the transformation.

From the diagram we see that i′=[12] and j′=[−1−1].

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is

T=[1−12−1].

Question 10
?

In the diagram above, i and j are the vectors of the standard basis of R2, while i′ and j′ are their images under the linear transformation T. What is the standard matrix of T?

a
[132−3]
b
[123−3]
c
[31−32]
d
[312−3]
e
[3−312]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Every linear transformation in R2 can be represented as a 2×2 matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors i and j under the action of the transformation.

From the diagram we see that i′=[3−3] and j′=[12].

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is

T=[31−32].

**Method 1**

The images of the vectors in the standard basis $\{ \mathbf{i}, \mathbf{j} \}$ are the first and second columns of $T,$ respectively. 

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(i) & =T[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 8\end{aligned}] \\ T(j) & =T[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

**Method 2**

We can find the images of the vectors in the standard basis $\{ \mathbf{i}, \mathbf{j} \}$ by computing the matrix products $T\cdot\mathbf{i}$ and $T\cdot\mathbf{j}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(i) & =T\cdot i=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 5 \\ 8 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 8\end{aligned}] \\ T(j) & =T\cdot j=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 5 \\ 8 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Question 11
?

The linear transformation T has the standard matrix T=[30−72]. What are the respective images of the standard basis vectors {i,j} of R2 under the action of T?

a
[32] and [0−7]
b
[02] and [3−7]
c
[−72] and [30]
d
[3−7] and [02]
e
[30] and [−72]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Method 1

The images of the vectors in the standard basis {i,j} are the first and second columns of T, respectively.

Therefore, we have the following:

T(i)=T[10]=[3−7]T(j)=T[01]=[02]

Method 2

We can find the images of the vectors in the standard basis {i,j} by computing the matrix products T⋅i and T⋅j:

T(i)=T⋅i=[30−72][10]=[3−7]T(j)=T⋅j=[30−72][01]=[02]

question.html:
Question 12
?

The linear transformation T has the standard matrix T=[5−2341−58−13]. What are the respective images of the standard basis vectors {i,j,k} of R3 under the action of T?

a
 [548], [−2−11], and [3−53]
b
 [5−23], [41−5], and [8−13]
c
 [584], [−2−11], and [33−5]
d
 [548], [−21−1], and [3−53]
e
 [5−23], [4−15], and [813]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Method 1

The images of the vectors in the standard basis {i,j,k} are the first, second, and third columns of T, respectively.

Therefore, we have the following:

T(i)=T[100]=[548]T(j)=T[010]=[−21−1]T(k)=T[001]=[3−53]

Method 2

We can find the images of the vectors in the standard basis {i,j,k} by computing the matrix products T⋅i, T⋅j, and T⋅k:

T(i)=T⋅i=[5−2341−58−13][100]=[548]T(j)=T⋅j=[5−2341−58−13][010]=[−21−1]T(k)=T⋅k=[5−2341−58−13][001]=[3−53]

**Method 1**

The images of the vectors in the standard basis $\{i,j\}$ are the first and second columns of $T,$ respectively. 

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(i) & =T[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\ T(j) & =T[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

**Method 2**

We can find the images of the vectors in the standard basis $\{i,j\}$ by computing the matrix products $T\cdot i$ and $T\cdot j:$

$$
\begin{aligned}T(i) & =T\cdot i=[\begin{aligned}4 & -4 \\ 5 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\ T(j) & =T\cdot j=[\begin{aligned}4 & -4 \\ 5 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem:
The linear transformation $T$ has the standard matrix 

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}4 & -4 \\ 5 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

 
What are the respective images of the standard basis vectors $\{i,j\}$ of ${R}^{2}$ under the action of $T?$
question.worked_solution:
**Method 1**

The images of the vectors in the standard basis $\{i,j\}$ are the first and second columns of $T,$ respectively. 

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(i) & =T[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\ T(j) & =T[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

**Method 2**

We can find the images of the vectors in the standard basis $\{i,j\}$ by computing the matrix products $T\cdot i$ and $T\cdot j:$

$$
\begin{aligned}T(i) & =T\cdot i=[\begin{aligned}4 & -4 \\ 5 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\ T(j) & =T\cdot j=[\begin{aligned}4 & -4 \\ 5 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

Question 13
?

The linear transformation T has the standard matrix T=[4−451]. What are the respective images of the standard basis vectors {i,j} of R2 under the action of T?

a
 [−45] and [41]
b
 [4−4] and [51]
c
 [45] and [−41]
d
 [41] and [−45]
e
 [−41] and [45]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Method 1

The images of the vectors in the standard basis {i,j} are the first and second columns of T, respectively.

Therefore, we have the following:

T(i)=T[10]=[45]T(j)=T[01]=[−41]

Method 2

We can find the images of the vectors in the standard basis {i,j} by computing the matrix products T⋅i and T⋅j:

T(i)=T⋅i=[4−451][10]=[45]T(j)=T⋅j=[4−451][01]=[−41]

question.html:
Question 14
?

The linear transformation T has the standard matrix T=[1−4−1−35−20−10]. What are the respective images of the standard basis vectors {i,j,k} of R3 under the action of T?

a
[−35−2], [1−4−1], and [0−10]
b
[−45−1], [1−30], and [−1−20]
c
[−310], [5−4−1], and [−2−10]
d
[1−30], [−45−1], and [−1−20]
e
[1−4−1], [−35−2], and [0−10]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Method 1

The images of the vectors in the standard basis {i,j,k} are the first, second, and third columns of T, respectively.

Therefore, we have the following:

T(i)=T[100]=[1−30]T(j)=T[010]=[−45−1]T(k)=T[001]=[−1−20]

Method 2

We can find the images of the vectors in the standard basis {i,j,k} by computing the matrix products T⋅i, T⋅j, and T⋅k:

T(i)=T⋅i=[1−4−1−35−20−10][100]=[1−30]T(j)=T⋅j=[1−4−1−35−20−10][010]=[−45−1]T(k)=T⋅k=[1−4−1−35−20−10][001]=[−1−20]

**Method 1**

The images of the vectors in the standard basis $\{i,j,k\}$ are the first, second, and third columns of $T,$ respectively. 

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(i) & =T[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ T(j) & =T[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ T(k) & =T[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

**Method 2**

We can find the images of the vectors in the standard basis $\{i,j,k\}$ by computing the matrix products $T\cdot i,$ $T\cdot j,$ and $T\cdot k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}T(i) & =T\cdot i=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 \\ 4 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ T(j) & =T\cdot j=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 \\ 4 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ T(k) & =T\cdot k=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 \\ 4 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 15
?

The linear transformation T has the standard matrix T=[1−2341−1110]. What are the respective images of the standard basis vectors {i,j,k} of R3 under the action of T?

a
 [114], [−211], and [30−1]
b
 [141], [−211], and [3−10]
c
 [141], [2−11], and [310]
d
 [123], [41−1], and [110]
e
 [1−23], [41−1], and [110]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Method 1

The images of the vectors in the standard basis {i,j,k} are the first, second, and third columns of T, respectively.

Therefore, we have the following:

T(i)=T[100]=[141]T(j)=T[010]=[−211]T(k)=T[001]=[3−10]

Method 2

We can find the images of the vectors in the standard basis {i,j,k} by computing the matrix products T⋅i, T⋅j, and T⋅k:

T(i)=T⋅i=[1−2341−1110][100]=[141]T(j)=T⋅j=[1−2341−1110][010]=[−211]T(k)=T⋅k=[1−2341−1110][001]=[3−10]

question.name: Question 1
question.problem: Given that $\{i,j,k\}$ is the standard basis of ${R}^{3}$ and that the images of $i,$ $j,$ and $k$ under the action of a linear transformation $T$ are $⟨2,-1,6⟩,$ $⟨7,2,0⟩,$ and $⟨1,-4,6⟩,$ respectively, what is the standard matrix of $T?$
question.worked_solution:
Every linear transformation in ${R}^{3}$ can be represented as a $3\times 3$ matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors $i,j,$ and $k$ under the action of the transformation.

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is 

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}2 & 7 & 1 \\ -1 & 2 & -4 \\ 6 & 0 & 6\end{aligned}].
$$

question.html:
Question 1
?

Given that {i,j,k} is the standard basis of R3 and that the images of i, j, and k under the action of a linear transformation T are ⟨2,−1,6⟩, ⟨7,2,0⟩, and ⟨1,−4,6⟩, respectively, what is the standard matrix of T?

a
 [271−142606]
b
 [271−12−4606]
c
 [2−167201−46]
d
 [271−124606]
e
 [217−1−42660]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Every linear transformation in R3 can be represented as a 3×3 matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors i,j, and k under the action of the transformation.

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is T=[271−12−4606].
question.knowledge_point: Determining the Standard Matrix of a Linear Transformation Given the Image of the Standard Basis

last_observation.worked_solution:
Every linear transformation in ${R}^{3}$ can be represented as a $3\times 3$ matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors $i,j,$ and $k$ under the action of the transformation.

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is 

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}2 & 7 & 1 \\ -1 & 2 & -4 \\ 6 & 0 & 6\end{aligned}].
$$

question.name: Question 1
question.problem: Given that $\{i,j,k\}$ is the standard basis of ${R}^{3}$ and that the images of $i,$ $j,$ and $k$ under the action of a linear transformation $T$ are $⟨2,-1,6⟩,$ $⟨7,2,0⟩,$ and $⟨1,-4,6⟩,$ respectively, what is the standard matrix of $T?$
question.worked_solution:
Every linear transformation in ${R}^{3}$ can be represented as a $3\times 3$ matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors $i,j,$ and $k$ under the action of the transformation.

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is 

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}2 & 7 & 1 \\ -1 & 2 & -4 \\ 6 & 0 & 6\end{aligned}].
$$

question.html:
Question 1
?

Given that {i,j,k} is the standard basis of R3 and that the images of i, j, and k under the action of a linear transformation T are ⟨2,−1,6⟩, ⟨7,2,0⟩, and ⟨1,−4,6⟩, respectively, what is the standard matrix of T?

a
 [271−142606]
b
 [271−12−4606]
c
 [2−167201−46]
d
 [271−124606]
e
 [217−1−42660]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Every linear transformation in R3 can be represented as a 3×3 matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors i,j, and k under the action of the transformation.

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is T=[271−12−4606].
question.knowledge_point: Determining the Standard Matrix of a Linear Transformation Given the Image of the Standard Basis

solution.reasoning: The standard matrix has T(i), T(j), and T(k) as its first, second, and third columns. Thus its rows are (2,7,1), (-1,2,-4), and (6,0,6), matching option b. The captured example supports this method, but no Math Academy answer or grade for the current question is provided.

feedback.name: Question 1
feedback.problem: Given that $\{i,j,k\}$ is the standard basis of ${R}^{3}$ and that the images of $i,$ $j,$ and $k$ under the action of a linear transformation $T$ are $⟨2,-1,6⟩,$ $⟨7,2,0⟩,$ and $⟨1,-4,6⟩,$ respectively, what is the standard matrix of $T?$
feedback.worked_solution:
Every linear transformation in ${R}^{3}$ can be represented as a $3\times 3$ matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors $i,j,$ and $k$ under the action of the transformation.

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is 

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}2 & 7 & 1 \\ -1 & 2 & -4 \\ 6 & 0 & 6\end{aligned}].
$$

Question 1
?

Given that {i,j,k} is the standard basis of R3 and that the images of i, j, and k under the action of a linear transformation T are ⟨2,−1,6⟩, ⟨7,2,0⟩, and ⟨1,−4,6⟩, respectively, what is the standard matrix of T?

a
 [271−142606]
b
 [271−12−4606]
c
 [2−167201−46]
d
 [271−124606]
e
 [217−1−42660]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Every linear transformation in R3 can be represented as a 3×3 matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors i,j, and k under the action of the transformation.

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is T=[271−12−4606].

question.name: Question 2
question.problem: Given that $\{i,j\}$ is the standard basis of ${R}^{2}$ and that the images of $i$ and $j$ under the action of a linear transformation $T$ are $⟨1,-1⟩$ and $⟨2,3⟩$, respectively, what is the standard matrix of $T?$
question.worked_solution:
Every linear transformation in ${R}^{2}$ can be represented as a $2\times 2$ matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors $i$ and $j$ under the action of the transformation.

Therefore, the standard matrix for this linear transformation is 

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

question.html:
Question 2
?

Given that {i,j} is the standard basis of R2 and that the images of i and j under the action of a linear transformation T are ⟨1,−1⟩ and ⟨2,3⟩, respectively, what is the standard matrix of T?

a
 [213−1]
b
 [12−13]
c
 [−1213]
d
 [13−12]
e
 [1−123]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Every linear transformation in R2 can be represented as a 2×2 matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors i and j under the action of the transformation.

Therefore, the standard matrix for this linear transformation is T=[12−13].

question.name: Question 2
question.problem: Given that $\{i,j\}$ is the standard basis of ${R}^{2}$ and that the images of $i$ and $j$ under the action of a linear transformation $T$ are $⟨1,-1⟩$ and $⟨2,3⟩$, respectively, what is the standard matrix of $T?$
question.worked_solution:
Every linear transformation in ${R}^{2}$ can be represented as a $2\times 2$ matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors $i$ and $j$ under the action of the transformation.

Therefore, the standard matrix for this linear transformation is 

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Question 2
?

Given that {i,j} is the standard basis of R2 and that the images of i and j under the action of a linear transformation T are ⟨1,−1⟩ and ⟨2,3⟩, respectively, what is the standard matrix of T?

a
 [213−1]
b
 [12−13]
c
 [−1213]
d
 [13−12]
e
 [1−123]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Every linear transformation in R2 can be represented as a 2×2 matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors i and j under the action of the transformation.

Therefore, the standard matrix for this linear transformation is T=[12−13].

a
 [213−1]
b
 [12−13]
c
 [−1213]
d
 [13−12]
e
 [1−123]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Every linear transformation in R2 can be represented as a 2×2 matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors i and j under the action of the transformation.

question.name: Question 3
question.problem: Given that $\{i,j\}$ is the standard basis of ${R}^{2}$ and that the images of $i$ and $j$ under the action of a linear transformation $T$ are $⟨2,4⟩$ and $⟨1,-5⟩$, respectively, what is the standard matrix of $T?$
question.worked_solution:
Every linear transformation in ${R}^{2}$ can be represented as a $2\times 2$ matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors $i$ and $j$ under the action of the transformation.

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 4 & -5\end{aligned}].
$$

question.html:
Question 3
?

Given that {i,j} is the standard basis of R2 and that the images of i and j under the action of a linear transformation T are ⟨2,4⟩ and ⟨1,−5⟩, respectively, what is the standard matrix of T?

a
 [2451]
b
 [214−5]
c
 [2−145]
d
 [241−5]
e
 [12−54]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Every linear transformation in R2 can be represented as a 2×2 matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors i and j under the action of the transformation.

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is
T=[214−5].

feedback.problem: Given that $\{i,j\}$ is the standard basis of ${R}^{2}$ and that the images of $i$ and $j$ under the action of a linear transformation $T$ are $⟨2,4⟩$ and $⟨1,-5⟩$, respectively, what is the standard matrix of $T?$
feedback.worked_solution:
Every linear transformation in ${R}^{2}$ can be represented as a $2\times 2$ matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors $i$ and $j$ under the action of the transformation.

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 4 & -5\end{aligned}].
$$

question.html:
Question 4
?

Given that {i,j,k} is the standard basis of R3 and that the images of i, j, and k under the action of a linear transformation T are ⟨6,2,0⟩, ⟨−3,5,6⟩, and ⟨−1,2,7⟩, respectively, what is the standard matrix of T?

a
[6−3−1252067]
b
[0672526−3−1]
c
[0676−3−1252]
d
[620−356−127]
e
[−127−356620]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Every linear transformation in R3 can be represented as a 3×3 matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors i,j, and k under the action of the transformation.

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is T=[6−3−1252067].
question.knowledge_point: Determining the Standard Matrix of a Linear Transformation Given the Image of the Standard Basis

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Determining the Standard Matrix of a Linear Transformation Given the Image of the Standard Basis

last_observation.worked_solution:
Every linear transformation in ${R}^{3}$ can be represented as a $3\times 3$ matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors $i,j,$ and $k$ under the action of the transformation.

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is 

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}6 & -3 & -1 \\ 2 & 5 & 2 \\ 0 & 6 & 7\end{aligned}].
$$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem: Given that $\{i,j,k\}$ is the standard basis of ${R}^{3}$ and that the images of $i,$ $j,$ and $k$ under the action of a linear transformation $T$ are $⟨6,2,0⟩,$ $⟨-3,5,6⟩,$ and $⟨-1,2,7⟩,$ respectively, what is the standard matrix of $T?$
question.worked_solution:
Every linear transformation in ${R}^{3}$ can be represented as a $3\times 3$ matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors $i,j,$ and $k$ under the action of the transformation.

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is 

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}6 & -3 & -1 \\ 2 & 5 & 2 \\ 0 & 6 & 7\end{aligned}].
$$

question.html:
Question 4
?

Given that {i,j,k} is the standard basis of R3 and that the images of i, j, and k under the action of a linear transformation T are ⟨6,2,0⟩, ⟨−3,5,6⟩, and ⟨−1,2,7⟩, respectively, what is the standard matrix of T?

a
[6−3−1252067]
b
[0672526−3−1]
c
[0676−3−1252]
d
[620−356−127]
e
[−127−356620]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Every linear transformation in R3 can be represented as a 3×3 matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors i,j, and k under the action of the transformation.

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is T=[6−3−1252067].
question.knowledge_point: Determining the Standard Matrix of a Linear Transformation Given the Image of the Standard Basis

solution.reasoning: The standard matrix places T(i)=(6,2,0), T(j)=(-3,5,6), and T(k)=(-1,2,7) in its columns, in that order. This gives option a. The mathematical answer is certain, but no Math Academy answer or grade for this question is captured.

feedback.name: Question 4
feedback.problem: Given that $\{i,j,k\}$ is the standard basis of ${R}^{3}$ and that the images of $i,$ $j,$ and $k$ under the action of a linear transformation $T$ are $⟨6,2,0⟩,$ $⟨-3,5,6⟩,$ and $⟨-1,2,7⟩,$ respectively, what is the standard matrix of $T?$
feedback.worked_solution:
Every linear transformation in ${R}^{3}$ can be represented as a $3\times 3$ matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors $i,j,$ and $k$ under the action of the transformation.

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is 

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}6 & -3 & -1 \\ 2 & 5 & 2 \\ 0 & 6 & 7\end{aligned}].
$$

Question 4
?

Given that {i,j,k} is the standard basis of R3 and that the images of i, j, and k under the action of a linear transformation T are ⟨6,2,0⟩, ⟨−3,5,6⟩, and ⟨−1,2,7⟩, respectively, what is the standard matrix of T?

a
[6−3−1252067]
b
[0672526−3−1]
c
[0676−3−1252]
d
[620−356−127]
e
[−127−356620]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Every linear transformation in R3 can be represented as a 3×3 matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors i,j, and k under the action of the transformation.

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is T=[6−3−1252067].

question.name: Question 5
question.problem: Given that $\{i,j\}$ is the standard basis of ${R}^{2}$ and that the images of $i$ and $j$ under the action of a linear transformation $T$ are $⟨1,4⟩$ and $⟨5,-1⟩$, respectively, what is the standard matrix of $T?$
question.worked_solution:
Every linear transformation in ${R}^{2}$ can be represented as a $2\times 2$ matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors $i$ and $j$ under the action of the transformation.

Therefore, the standard matrix for this linear transformation is 

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}1 & 5 \\ 4 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

question.html:
Question 5
?

Given that {i,j} is the standard basis of R2 and that the images of i and j under the action of a linear transformation T are ⟨1,4⟩ and ⟨5,−1⟩, respectively, what is the standard matrix of T?

a
 [1451]
b
 [−1541]
c
 [154−1]
d
 [15−41]
e
 [145−1]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Every linear transformation in R2 can be represented as a 2×2 matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors i and j under the action of the transformation.

Therefore, the standard matrix for this linear transformation is T=[154−1].

question.html:
Question 5
?

Given that {i,j} is the standard basis of R2 and that the images of i and j under the action of a linear transformation T are ⟨1,4⟩ and ⟨5,−1⟩, respectively, what is the standard matrix of T?

a
 [1451]
b
 [−1541]
c
 [154−1]
d
 [15−41]
e
 [145−1]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Every linear transformation in R2 can be represented as a 2×2 matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors i and j under the action of the transformation.

Therefore, the standard matrix for this linear transformation is T=[154−1].
question.knowledge_point: Determining the Standard Matrix of a Linear Transformation Given the Image of the Standard Basis

solution.reasoning: The standard matrix has T(i)=(1,4) as its first column and T(j)=(5,-1) as its second column, giving option c. The mathematical answer is certain, but no Math Academy answer or grade for this question is captured.

feedback.name: Question 5
feedback.problem: Given that $\{i,j\}$ is the standard basis of ${R}^{2}$ and that the images of $i$ and $j$ under the action of a linear transformation $T$ are $⟨1,4⟩$ and $⟨5,-1⟩$, respectively, what is the standard matrix of $T?$
feedback.worked_solution:
Every linear transformation in ${R}^{2}$ can be represented as a $2\times 2$ matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors $i$ and $j$ under the action of the transformation.

Therefore, the standard matrix for this linear transformation is 

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}1 & 5 \\ 4 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14154685/assets/09423b097ab02b339f15af831e0e35f59ff88cb00c0ef72d3693ce9f24e6b9dc.png)

In the diagram above, $i$ and $j$ are the vectors of the standard basis of ${R}^{2}$, while ${i}^{′}$ and ${j}^{′}$ are their images under the linear transformation $T.$
What is the standard matrix of $T?$
question.worked_solution:
Every linear transformation in ${R}^{2}$ can be represented as a $2\times 2$ matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors $i$ and $j$ under the action of the transformation.

From the diagram we see that 
${i}^{′}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -3\end{aligned}]$ 
and 
${j}^{′}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is 

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ -3 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

[−2−313]

Question 6
?

In the diagram above, i and j are the vectors of the standard basis of R2, while i′ and j′ are their images under the linear transformation T. What is the standard matrix of T?

a
[13−2−3]
b
[1−2−33]
c
[1−23−3]
d
[−2−313]
e
[−21−33]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Every linear transformation in R2 can be represented as a 2×2 matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors i and j under the action of the transformation.

From the diagram we see that i′=[−2−3] and j′=[13].

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is

T=[−21−33].

a
[13−2−3]

[1−2−33]

[1−23−3]

[−2−313]
e
[−21−33]
Submit

Every linear transformation in R2 can be represented as a 2×2 matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors i and j under the action of the transformation.

From the diagram we see that i′=[−2−3] and j′=[13].

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is

T=[−21−33].

In the diagram above,  $i$ and $j$ are the vectors of the standard basis of ${R}^{2}$, while ${i}^{′}$ and  ${j}^{′}$ are their images under the linear transformation $T.$
What is the standard matrix of $T?$
question.worked_solution:
Every linear transformation in ${R}^{2}$ can be represented as a $2\times 2$ matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors $i$ and $j$ under the action of the transformation.

From the diagram we see that 
${i}^{′}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]$ 
and 
${j}^{′}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is 

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

question.html:
Question 7
?

In the diagram above, i and j are the vectors of the standard basis of R2, while i′ and j′ are their images under the linear transformation T. What is the standard matrix of T?

a
[−2231]
b
 [21−23]
c
 [−2123]
d
 [2−213]
e
 [−2321]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Every linear transformation in R2 can be represented as a 2×2 matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors i and j under the action of the transformation.

From the diagram we see that i′=[−23] and j′=[21].

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is

T=[−2231].

question.html:
Question 7
?

In the diagram above, i and j are the vectors of the standard basis of R2, while i′ and j′ are their images under the linear transformation T. What is the standard matrix of T?

a
[−2231]
b
 [21−23]
c
 [−2123]
d
 [2−213]
e
 [−2321]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Every linear transformation in R2 can be represented as a 2×2 matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors i and j under the action of the transformation.

From the diagram we see that i′=[−23] and j′=[21].

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is

T=[−2231].
question.knowledge_point: Determining the Standard Matrix of a Linear Transformation Given a Diagram

solution.reasoning: The current diagram shows i′=(-2,3) and j′=(2,1). Placing these images in the first and second columns gives option a. The mathematical answer is certain, but no Math Academy answer or grade for this question is captured.

feedback.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14154685/assets/5aaf29ab4dd2de3d104ca37a71ee66078f985b908465a77ca06ba8ffadd50210.png)

In the diagram above,  $i$ and $j$ are the vectors of the standard basis of ${R}^{2}$, while ${i}^{′}$ and  ${j}^{′}$ are their images under the linear transformation $T.$
What is the standard matrix of $T?$
feedback.worked_solution:
Every linear transformation in ${R}^{2}$ can be represented as a $2\times 2$ matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors $i$ and $j$ under the action of the transformation.

From the diagram we see that 
${i}^{′}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]$ 
and 
${j}^{′}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is 

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

a

 [−2123]

 [2−213]

 [−2321]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14154685/assets/ad1f032fd5b99252d348d0cf71308ef1de0f65f06ddd9070b569cff69bc506f9.png)

In the diagram above, $i$ and $j$ are the vectors of the standard basis of ${R}^{2}$, while ${i}^{′}$ and ${j}^{′}$ are their images under the linear transformation $T.$
What is the standard matrix of $T?$
question.worked_solution:
Every linear transformation in ${R}^{2}$ can be represented as a $2\times 2$ matrix. The standard matrix representation of the transformation has columns that are the images of the vectors $i$ and $j$ under the action of the transformation.

From the diagram we see that 
${i}^{′}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ 
and 
${j}^{′}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$

Therefore, the standard matrix for the linear transformation is 

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

 [112−1]
b
[1−12−1]
c
[−121−1]
d
 [−1−112]

 [12−1−1]
